description:
Surfaced 2026-08-04 while verifying ub-lp9.27, and scoped out of it because nothing in that change causes it.

`LibsqlStorage::open_in_memory` opens a shared-cache URI, which mutates SQLite's process-global shared-cache registry. Its own doc comment (around `crates/unblock-storage/src/libsql/mod.rs:326-346`) already documents the consequence: an internal open-lock serializes open-against-open but explicitly "cannot cover the window where an open races a concurrent large shared-cache transaction", and the class is described as "a load-marginal artifact of the shared-cache registry, not a bug this constructor can safely immunize against".

The practical cost is that a REQUIRED CI job can go red for a reason that has nothing to do with the change being tested, and a reviewer then has to prove a negative under time pressure. That is exactly what happened during the ub-lp9.27 verification, and closing it took two independent controlled experiments.

WHAT WAS MEASURED THERE, worth keeping because it bounds the problem rather than merely naming it:
- Every observed failure landed at the store OPEN (the fixture helper around `crates/unblock-storage/tests/behaviour.rs:29`), never at an assertion, and always in tests unrelated to the change under test.
- One controlled comparison: 1 failure in 25 behaviour-suite executions with the change, and 1 in 60 with the change's new test removed — the same rate band on both sides, i.e. no attributable effect.
- A second: 15 full workspace executions across three legs, one of them carrying 40 times the marginal load the change added, with ZERO failures — the class could not be reproduced at all on that machine.

The doc comment already prescribes a direction (route heavy or high-concurrency work through the file-backed constructor instead). The open question this issue exists to answer is whether the behaviour suite as a whole should migrate, or whether a narrower fix reaches the same result.

### Acceptance Criteria
- A decision is recorded on whether the behaviour suite migrates off the shared-cache in-memory constructor, with the reasoning — including what the in-memory constructor is buying today (speed, isolation) and what migrating would cost.
- Whatever is chosen is measured rather than asserted: a failure-rate comparison across enough executions to distinguish the rates involved, given the observed base rate is on the order of one in tens of runs.
- If the class survives by design, the required job's failure is made SELF-EXPLAINING — whoever meets a red run learns from the output that this class exists and how to tell it apart from a real regression, rather than having to rediscover the doc comment.
title: The shared-cache in-memory store can redden the required workspace-test job for reasons unrelated to the change under test

description:
Raised 2026-08-04 by the Verify gate on ub-lp9.27, scoped out of that change because it is a question about a rule rather than a defect in the fix.

The interface spine states normatively that the label reconcile INSERT stays STRICT — never ignore-on-conflict — so that the label uniqueness constraint remains a loud tripwire if the diff base ever regresses. That rule was a deliberate ruling on ub-lp9.27, and the reasoning behind it stands.

The problem is that the rule is pinned by NOTHING, and appears to be unpinnable by construction. A mutation relaxing the INSERT to ignore-on-conflict left both the contract suite and the behaviour suite green, and the gate coordinator judged it a semantically EQUIVALENT mutant rather than a coverage hole, verified by reading the code: with a correct diff base the additions set can only ever name labels absent from the table, so no conflict is reachable and the two spellings cannot differ in observable behaviour. A compound experiment confirmed the tripwire still works as intended — relaxing the INSERT while ALSO reintroducing the diff-base bug still reddened every relevant case, through different assertions.

So the honest position is that the rule buys a louder failure mode in a future regression, and that no test can distinguish it from its alternative today. That is a legitimate thing for a codebase to conclude, but it should be CONCLUDED rather than left as an unexamined gap — otherwise a future reader finds a normative rule with no enforcement and reasonably assumes someone forgot to write the test.

### Acceptance Criteria
- A decision is recorded on whether the strict-INSERT rule is testable: either a test lands that genuinely distinguishes strict from ignore-on-conflict, or the conclusion that it cannot be distinguished through the trait surface is written down with the reasoning.
- If it cannot be, the code comment beside that INSERT says so explicitly — that it is the only guard, and why the rule is kept anyway — so the absence of a test reads as a considered position rather than an omission.
- The spine sentence is left consistent with whatever is decided.
title: Decide whether the spine's strict label INSERT rule is testable at all — and if not, say so where the only guard lives

description:
Found 2026-08-06 by the ub-cnv (D47) Verify gate, whose adversarial lens measured it rather than reasoned about it. Miguel scoped it OUT of D47 and into its own issue: it is PRE-EXISTING, not a regression, and the real fix touches a transport seam D47 deliberately left alone.

MECHANISM, confirmed at source by two independent readers. rmcp drives our transport's receive() as one arm of a tokio select! with no priority (rmcp-1.7.0/src/service.rs:805, the receive arm at :813), so that future is DROPPED whenever another arm wins the race. Both out-of-band replies our transport emits are written INSIDE receive(): the pre-existing -32700 parse-error arm, and the -32600 arm D47 added (crates/unblock-mcp/src/wire.rs). On cancellation the reply is therefore never written — and the frame is lost too, because the next iteration begins by clearing the line buffer. There is no retry and no queue.

MEASURED, once, by one harness, and recorded as such rather than dressed up: 0 of 40 replies lost on an idle connection; 25 of 40 lost with four concurrent requests in flight; 39 of 40 lost with eight. The pre-existing -32700 arm on main loses at the same rate (35 of 40 at eight), which is what establishes this as a property of the transport rather than of D47.

WHY IT WAS NOT FIXED IN D47, and why that was right. It is outside the decided scope of that change; the severe case D47 exists to remove — the frame that killed the process before the handshake — occurs by definition with zero requests in flight, the regime measured at zero losses; and fixing it properly means changing where the transport writes, which would drag the pre-existing -32700 arm along with it or leave two different behaviours in one file. D47 discloses the residual instead of claiming a guarantee it does not hold under load (docs/PRD.md, the D47 row; crates/unblock-mcp/src/wire.rs module documentation).

DO NOT let the mutex around the write half be mistaken for a defence: it buys byte-atomicity between concurrent writers, which is a different property entirely from surviving future cancellation.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- The loss is reproduced deliberately and the rates are REPLICATED by a second harness, since the recorded figures are single-run and single-harness.
- The transport stops writing replies from inside receive(): the reply is parked on the transport itself, or pushed to whatever sink send() already uses, so a cancelled receive() cannot swallow it.
- BOTH out-of-band arms move together — the -32600 envelope-id arm and the pre-existing -32700 parse-error arm — so the file does not end up with two behaviours.
- A regression cell drives concurrent traffic and asserts the reply arrives; it must fail on the current code.
- The residual disclosures land closed: the D47 decision row, the transport module documentation, and both roadmap cards stop naming this as open.
title: Bug: an out-of-band transport reply is lost whenever rmcp cancels the receive() future under concurrent request traffic

description:
Split out of ub-b1a by Miguel's decision at its Decide phase (2026-09-09). ub-b1a bounds what the startup-failure diagnostic RENDERS about a rejected first frame; this issue is about what the server READS, which is a different question with a different blast radius.

WHAT IT IS. The owned stdio transport `DupScanningTransport` (crates/unblock-mcp/src/wire.rs:189-190) reads each frame with `read_until(b'\n', ..)` and states in its own doc comment that "there is deliberately no line-length bound here, exactly as rmcp has none (`max_length: usize::MAX`)". So a single line of any size (5,000,000 bytes was measured for ub-b1a, off main at 4f0ab59) is buffered whole, then parsed TWICE (the D43 duplicate-key scan and the serde parse), before any handler runs. `Quotas::max_request_bytes` (crates/unblock-mcp/src/options.rs) binds only inside `call_tool`, after the parse, and never before the `initialize` handshake.

WHY IT IS ITS OWN DECISION. A read cap changes what the server ACCEPTS, not what it prints: a conforming client with a legitimately large `tools/call` (a bulk markdown document under the NFR-18 quota, for instance) must never be rejected below the quota it is promised, and a line that exceeds the cap needs a defined reply (a JSON-RPC error on the recovered id, or answer-and-drop like the D47 arm, or a disconnect). That is a new decision row with its own acceptance criteria, and it touches the CD-7 differential harness (crates/unblock-mcp/src/wire.rs, the parity corpus) because rmcp itself has no such cap.

RELATION. ub-b1a (the render bound, closed by the decision that names this issue) removes the amplification of the diagnostic but not the memory cost of buffering the line. ub-5v5 (no RESPONSE-size cap) is the outbound sibling. NFR-18 is the quota surface that would state the inbound bound.

FIRST STEP. Decide the bound's relation to the existing `Quotas` (a single inbound line bound at least as large as `max_request_bytes` plus envelope overhead is the natural anchor), and what the server replies with above it. Then implement at the transport read, with the harness parity cases updated deliberately rather than silently.
title: Finding: the stdio transport reads a frame line with no length bound (rmcp parity); a read cap needs its own decision

acceptance_criteria:
REWRITTEN at the Decide/Spec boundary and CORRECTED at the design Review gate (2026-08-06). The original four criteria are superseded because two were unsatisfiable-as-meant: "all four Err sources" is vacuously satisfiable (two of the four return sites are structurally unreachable), and "stdout carries only JSON-RPC frames for the whole process lifetime" literally covers `unblock mcp --help`, which the Decide phase ruled explicitly out. The substance is unchanged and nothing is narrowed.

1. CHANNEL. On `unblock mcp`, no failure of the command may put a non-frame byte on stdout. Proven over the REACHABLE failure cases, named individually rather than counted: the walk-up workspace miss (`NOT_INITIALIZED`, exit 2), an explicit `--dir`/`UNBLOCK_DIR` at a non-workspace (`CONFIG_ERROR`, exit 7), a rejected `UNBLOCK_OUTPUT_FORMAT` (`CONFIG_ERROR`, exit 7), a database newer than the build (`SCHEMA_MISMATCH`, exit 2), a corrupt database (`DATABASE_ERROR`, exit 2), and a first frame that is neither `initialize` nor `ping` (`INTERNAL_ERROR`, exit 1 — `ping` is answered pre-handshake and is NOT a failure case; see the gate comment). The two unreachable return sites (`Session::open`, which fails only on a feature the CLI hard-codes off, and the teardown, whose semaphore is never closed) are documented as unreachable rather than covered by a cell that can only pass vacuously.

2. POSITIVE LANDING, not only the absence. Every case above must ALSO be shown to land the full structured document on stderr — `code`, `message`, `retryable`, and `hint` where the code carries one. A frame-only negative alone is insufficient and is explicitly rejected as an acceptance route: on the pre-run-loop cases stdout is legitimately empty, so a negative-only assertion stays green under a delete-the-diagnostic mutation. That vacuity class is what hid this defect.

3. EXIT CODES UNMOVED. Every code listed in criterion 1 is the code that ships. A failed handshake keeps exit 1; the reconciliation with D40 is that D40's exit-0 carve-out covers the pre-`initialize` DISCONNECT only and is untouched, and that after the GA tag a one-to-zero flip on this surface would be a semver-relevant CLI change under D35.

4. MUTATION PROOF. Every cell added or inverted names the concrete source edit that turns it red, and that edit is actually applied and observed to turn it red — a coverage claim is not accepted on inspection. This binds especially the swapped-sink mutation, which compiles and survives every in-process cell, and is why a spawning end-to-end cell is required alongside the injected sinks.

5. THE INVERSIONS ARE HONEST, AND FAIL LOUD. The two shipped cells that assert the defect as correct (`crates/unblock-cli/tests/mcp_lifecycle.rs:429-440` and `:602-606`, coupled at `:578-583`) are rewritten to assert the new channel while still pinning what they protected — the exit code, the never-swallowed clause, and the D47 coupling. No cell is weakened to make it pass. AND the harness drain handles are retained and joined before any negative stdout snapshot: without that, an inverted "stdout is empty" assertion goes GREEN on a lost race where today's positive assertion goes red, turning this change's own regression pins fail-silent.

6. THE CLASS THAT HID IT IS CLOSED. The shared stream guard (`crates/unblock-cli/tests/common/mod.rs:324-326`) requires a top-level `jsonrpc` member rather than merely valid JSON, that guard is itself driven by a self-test (a guard nobody drives is a guard that can be deleted), and the shared spawn helper (`:111-117`) scrubs `UNBLOCK_OUTPUT_FORMAT` — without which any new frame-only cell passes vacuously from a host shell that sets it.

7. NFR-14 RECONCILED, D48 LANDED. The decision ships as D48 with reciprocal cross-references to the D38 clause it supersedes, the NFR-14 carve-out stated over the PROPERTY (a subcommand whose stdout is a protocol channel) and not over a command name, and the D-range bump at every live site PROCESS section 3 enumerates. `unblock mcp --help` is ruled out of scope IN THE DECISION TEXT, and the carve-out is carried into NFR-14 and the README too — not only into the decision row a casual reader never reaches.

8. NOTHING ELSE MOVES. No other subcommand's bytes change stream; no MCP contract byte, `CONTRACT_HASH` or `ErrorCode` moves; no layer edge changes. Proven, not asserted.

9. THE GATE SCRIPT. D48 mints `scripts/checks/d48-stdout-channel-claims.sh`, following the D44/D45/D46/D47 precedent, in the IMPLEMENTATION commit together with the prose that enumerates it as a required step (ci-cd section 2.1, PROCESS section 3, the CI workflow). It pins what prose alone cannot: the residual-issue landing duty and the single-caller invariant the mechanism leans on.

10. RESIDUALS DISCLOSED, not implied closed. Four are named in the decision row as deliberately open: `ub-kp7` (a first frame that is neither `initialize` nor `ping` still kills the server), `ub-b1a` (the message still embeds an unbounded `Debug` rendering of client bytes), `ub-c5o` (`output::emit_report` writes to stdout with no notion of a stdout-owning command — latent), and `ub-5v5` (no response-size cap, so a large frame may be written truncated — reasoned from source, never reproduced). Unmeasured classes — a blob following valid frames via a panic in the spawned serve task, Windows, and a non-pipe descriptor 1 — are stated as unmeasured rather than covered.
close_reason: Merged to main via PR 439 (2026-08-07, rebase-merge, tip 9adc2cb) as decision D48. The `unblock mcp` structured error no longer lands on STDOUT, which on the MCP stdio transport is the JSON-RPC framing channel: the exit boundary now knows that a command owns stdout as a protocol channel and writes the FULL structured document — code, message, retryable and hint — to stderr instead. Exit codes are unmoved. The defect was five routes wide, not the one its report named, and the likeliest was the most mundane: a workspace open that fails before the startup binding line, leaving stdout with the blob and stderr completely empty. Measured after the fix: all six reachable routes put zero non-frame bytes on stdout with the document on stderr, newline-terminated, at exit 2/7/7/2/1/1; a pre-initialize ping is still answered into a normal handshake; clean EOF still exits 0; version and migrate still write to stdout. 17 named mutations killed including the swapped-sink one that survives every in-process cell, and an invented-mutation pass found five further unpinned claims, all closed. Both gates FAILED and neither was closed by a clean re-pass — the design gate by an orchestrator-applied third pass under the PROCESS section 5 escalation, the Verify gate by a narrow independent recheck plus orchestrator measurement, both on Miguel's explicit ruling; this is recorded rather than smoothed over. Four residuals disclosed rather than absorbed: ub-kp7 (a first frame that is neither initialize nor ping still kills the server), ub-b1a (the relocated message still carries an unbounded Debug rendering of client bytes, raised to high priority once the one-for-one amplification into a persistent log sink was measured), ub-c5o (emit_report still writes to stdout unclassified, latent), ub-5v5 (no response-size cap, reasoned from source and never reproduced). ub-gwe was raised in passing and is unrelated.

comments.author: ramosmig
comments.text:
Orchestrator orientation (2026-08-06), off main at 7790db0 (post-D47/PR 438), binary `target/debug/unblock` rebuilt.

Measured with a raw stdio probe: one spawn per case, frames fed on stdin, stdout and stderr captured separately, every stdout line parsed and checked for `"jsonrpc":"2.0"`. Script kept out of the repo. Cases are named, not lettered, so this comment stays readable on its own.

WHAT THE PROBE FOUND — the blob is NOT confined to the handshake path.

1. `pre-handshake notification first` (`notifications/cancelled` as the very first frame): stdout gets one non-frame line `{"code":"INTERNAL_ERROR","message":"mcp server error: failed to start the MCP server: expect initialized request ..."}`, exit 1. This is the issue's reproduction, still live.

2. `pre-handshake non-initialize REQUEST first` (`tools/list` with id 7): IDENTICAL blob on stdout, exit 1. This CORRECTS the issue description, which says a clean non-initialize request in that position is answered normally and exits 0. It is not: rmcp's `expect_next_message` rejects ANY non-`initialize` message in the initialize slot. The trigger is therefore not the degradation to a notification — it is any first frame that is not `initialize`.

3. `no workspace` (UNBLOCK_DIR pointing at a non-workspace): stdout gets a non-frame `{"code":"CONFIG_ERROR",...}` line, exit 7. This is a PRE-run-loop failure and, in practice, the most likely real-world one — it is what an MCP client sees whenever it spawns the server outside a workspace.

4. `corrupt db` (`.unblock/unblock.db` containing text): stdout gets a non-frame `{"code":"DATABASE_ERROR",...}` line, exit 2. Also pre-run-loop.

5. `EOF before any frame`: stdout empty, exit 0 — D40 holds.

6. `full handshake then EOF`: one valid frame, exit 0 — the healthy path is unaffected.

7. `garbage non-JSON first line`: answered in-band with a `-32700` parse-error frame, exit 0 — the D47/D43 wire seam behaves.

8. `pre-handshake notification with -o plain`: stdout EMPTY, the same error rendered as `error[INTERNAL_ERROR]: ...` on stderr, exit 1. So the stream is chosen purely by the resolved output format, and `UNBLOCK_OUTPUT_FORMAT=plain` is today an accidental workaround for the defect.

MECHANISM. Every error returned by `commands::mcp::run` reaches `run_with` → `exit::into_exit(err, fmt)` (crates/unblock-cli/src/lib.rs:78), and its json/robot arm (crates/unblock-cli/src/exit.rs:135-145) writes the structured payload to STDOUT. The resolved format defaults to Json (crates/unblock-cli/src/output.rs:173). So the blob is not one path but FOUR error sources on the mcp command, all sharing one renderer: the workspace open, `Session::open`, the run loop, and the teardown — the first two of which the issue text only suspected.

Everything the command emits deliberately already goes to stderr: the D39 workspace-binding line (crates/unblock-cli/src/commands/mcp.rs:273), the D38 `emit_diagnostic` line (crates/unblock-cli/src/exit.rs:171), tracing. The single leak is the terminal `into_exit` render.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR SCOPE. The exit-code question the acceptance criteria raise is separable from the channel question, and the channel question is the wider of the two: fixing only the handshake case would leave the two pre-run-loop cases (3 and 4) writing the same non-frame bytes onto the framing channel. The Understand phase is briefed to enumerate the remaining stdout writers exhaustively (panic path, rmcp internals, libsql, any direct print) rather than assume these four are all.

comments.author: ramosmig
comments.text:
DECIDE phase closed (2026-08-06). Understand ran as a four-lens team plus coordinator; the consolidated map was re-verified by the orchestrator against source before anything was put to Miguel. Miguel resolved four forks; the orchestrator ruled the rest. Both gates are still ahead.

WHAT THE UNDERSTAND PHASE CHANGED ABOUT THE PROBLEM
- The likeliest real-world hit is NOT the handshake: it is the workspace open failing (crates/unblock-cli/src/commands/mcp.rs:267), which puts a CONFIG_ERROR blob on stdout with exit 7 and leaves stderr COMPLETELY EMPTY — the D39 binding line at :273 runs only after the open succeeds. A schema-newer database and a corrupt database land the same way with exit 2, and a bad UNBLOCK_OUTPUT_FORMAT value is reported, self-referentially, in the format the resolver defaulted to.
- Of the four return sites, only two are reachable: Session::open fails only on FeatureNotWired for sync, which the CLI hard-codes off (crates/unblock-cli/src/dispatch.rs:48), and the teardown fails only on a poisoned write permit whose semaphore is never closed anywhere in the engine. An acceptance criterion phrased as "covers all four sources" would be satisfiable vacuously.
- Two SHIPPED test cells assert the defect as correct and must INVERT: crates/unblock-cli/tests/mcp_lifecycle.rs:429-440 (asserts the payload on stdout carries INTERNAL_ERROR, docstring at :404-406 calling it the FR-11 anchor) and :602-606, coupled by design at :578-583. The reason the suite never caught this: the only stream guard, crates/unblock-cli/tests/common/mod.rs:324-326, panics with the message "every stdout line must be JSON-RPC framing" but only calls serde_json::from_str — and the blob is valid JSON.

MIGUEL'S FORK RESOLUTIONS
1. Mechanism — the exit boundary learns that a command owns stdout. A predicate read where the parsed command is still in scope (crates/unblock-cli/src/lib.rs:73-75) is threaded into into_exit, whose machine-format arm then writes to stderr for such a command. Chosen over forcing the plain format (which would silently break the FR-13 precedence that pick_cli_format exists to implement) and over having mcp report its own errors (which would add a second exit-code-computing site against the rule that the CLI owns the cast, crates/unblock-cli/src/exit.rs:1-3).
2. Payload — the FULL structured JSON moves to stderr, not the one-line human form. Reason: it keeps the hint member, which is exactly what the schema-mismatch case (D46) carries, and it stays machine-readable for an MCP host that captures the child's stderr.
3. Resilience — the server surviving a non-initialize first frame is REAL work but its OWN task: ub-kp7. ub-og3 stays a pure channel fix.
4. Exit code — a failed handshake KEEPS exit 1. D40 records that after the GA tag a one-to-zero flip on this surface is a semver-relevant CLI change under D35, and D40 covers only the ConnectionClosed case, not this one. Consequence: the exit-code question does not move, so the new decision has a single clause and needs no second D-id.

ORCHESTRATOR RULINGS (Miguel invited objection; none raised)
5. `unblock mcp --help` is OUT of scope, explicitly rather than silently: it writes 846 bytes of prose to stdout with exit 0, but the server never starts, so the framing channel is never live; routing it to stderr would depart from clap and from every other subcommand. The decision states this rather than leaving it to re-open at the Verify gate. (Verified in passing that `unblock mcp --version` is a usage error to stderr with exit 2, correcting one lens that claimed otherwise.)
6. The regression test does BOTH: a spawning end-to-end cell AND an injected sink on into_exit. In-process capture is otherwise impossible — into_exit writes through std::io::stdout().lock(), bypassing libtest capture, and forbid(unsafe_code) with no libc dependency rules out redirecting the descriptor. The sink also closes the sibling hole at crates/unblock-cli/src/logging.rs:46, where mutating the writer to stdout survives the entire suite today. The test must assert a POSITIVE stderr landing, not only the frame-only negative: for the pre-run-loop cases stdout is legitimately empty, so a negative-only assertion stays green under "delete the diagnostic". UNBLOCK_OUTPUT_FORMAT must also be scrubbed in the shared spawn helper (crates/unblock-cli/tests/common/mod.rs:111-117 scrubs three variables but not that one) or a host shell setting it makes the new test pass vacuously.
7. The attacker-controlled Debug rendering in the message — the other half of D47 clause 8(iii) — goes to its own issue, ub-b1a. Control characters are already escaped by sanitize_message; what is unruled is the absence of a length cap.
8. Pre-run-loop failures KEEP their own 0-8 exit codes (7 for config, 2 for database). Only the channel moves. This preserves the D38 scope boundary, which explicitly places a failure raised before the run loop outside the cancellation's consequences.
9. The shared harness guard at crates/unblock-cli/tests/common/mod.rs:324-326 is hardened in this change to require a jsonrpc member, not merely valid JSON. It does not by itself catch this defect (the blob is written after the run loop, past that read path) but it closes the class that hid it, and roughly forty inherited cells then obey it.

DECISION IDENTITY — a NEW D-id (D48), not an addendum. PROCESS §3 puts a refinement whose intent is preserved on the addendum arm, expressly "not a reversal". This IS a reversal: docs/PRD.md:121 and docs/plans/01-design-spine.md:3333 affirmatively rule that FR-11's always-valid-JSON-on-stdout rule binds the unsignalled error path. PROCESS §3 then sends a clause reversal that falls out of a new decision to that decision's own D-id. Two independent supports: the pre-run-loop failures occupy ground no shipped decision row covers, and D47 clause 8(iii) has already classified this as a separate defect with its own issue. Consequences: reciprocal cross-references at both rows, and the D-range bump from D1..D47 to D1..D48 at all seven live sites in the same spec commit — CLAUDE.md:17, docs/plans/ci-cd-and-distribution.md:65, xtask/src/doc_lint.rs:455, and the range knobs of the four shipped required check scripts. The historical range strings inside docs/plans/implementation-plan.md:40,:53,:90 are past bump records and must NOT be re-bumped. A gap to close in the same commit: ub-og3 has no normative name anywhere — both docs/PRD.md:130 and the roadmap say "a separate defect with its own issue" without the id.

RESIDUALS CARRIED INTO SPEC/PLAN, not silently dropped: whether a blob can follow VALID frames (only via a panic in rmcp's spawned serve task, reasoned from source and never measured — if unreachable the acceptance criterion's "including teardown failures" has no live referent and should say so); the truncated frame above two mebibytes with no response-size cap, a different defect on the same channel; Windows, where every measurement here is macOS; and a non-pipe or closed descriptor 1, where write failures are swallowed by design.

comments.author: ramosmig
comments.text:
DESIGN REVIEW GATE — closed PASS after two adversarial rounds plus an orchestrator-applied third pass, under a PROCESS section 5 escalation Miguel ruled on directly (2026-08-06). Branch ub-og3-mcp-stdout-channel, spec-only, uncommitted at the time of writing.

ROUND 1 — FAIL, 15 must-fixes and 10 should-fixes. Four adversarial lenses (code claims, doc cascade, design soundness, test adequacy) plus a coordinator, run against a throwaway worktree so the live tree was never touched. The gate earned its cost: the findings were real and several were the exact class this repo has paid for before — prose asserting more than is true.

THE CORRECTION THAT MATTERED MOST, and it was the orchestrator's own error, repeated into three artifacts before the gate caught it. The claim "any first frame that is not `initialize` kills the server" is FALSE. A pre-`initialize` `ping` is ANSWERED and the server lives on to complete a normal handshake. Established twice over: read in rmcp 1.7.0 service/server.rs:170-204, where the loop answers a `PingRequest` at :175-189 and CONTINUES (the code comment cites the MCP lifecycle specification, which permits ping before initialize), breaks on any other Request at :191, errors on any non-Request at :193, and errors on a non-`initialize` Request at :200-204; and measured directly — a ping frame first is answered with an empty result, a following `initialize` completes, exit 0. The true class is "any first frame that is neither `initialize` nor `ping`, Request or Notification". The false version had already reached the orientation comment above, the ub-kp7 issue and the D48 row; all three are corrected.

OTHER ROUND-1 FINDINGS WORTH RECORDING, because each is a defect a lint cannot reach:
- NFR-14 and the README were left stating an ABSOLUTE ("stdout carries framing only") that a shipped green test falsifies — `unblock mcp --help` writes clap prose to stdout, which the decision's own clause deliberately excludes. The carve-out existed in the decision row but not in the two sentences a reader meets without it.
- A specified test guard whose body could never execute: every call site asserted stdout was empty immediately after calling the framing predicate, so replacing the predicate with an empty body left the whole matrix green.
- The two inversions would have converted a fail-LOUD race into a fail-SILENT one. The harness spawns a detached stdout drain thread and never joins it; today's positive assertion goes red when that race is lost, but the new "stdout is empty" assertion goes GREEN — so the headline mutation could survive on the stdout half of this change's own regression pins. The remedy is to retain and join the handle before any negative snapshot.
- A derived count wrong again ("all four return sites"; there are three — the fourth exists only as an error SOURCE, a different noun), a roadmap citation that named a slot holding something else, and the ub-b1a residual anchored in a file containing no `Debug` formatting at all.

ROUND 2 — FAIL, 4 must-fixes, all one-clause prose edits, two of them NEWLY INTRODUCED by round 2 itself. That is the honest signal: each pass fixes findings and writes new prose, and new prose carries new claims.

ESCALATION AND CLOSURE. PROCESS section 5 escalates after two iterations rather than looping. Miguel ruled the orchestrator applies the four by hand, since the judgement was already done and only the typing remained. All four verified against source first, then applied:
1. the row that MINTS ub-b1a still anchored it at the serialiser rather than at its origin, contradicting the line immediately below it in the same diff;
2. one crate-plan cell declared both the old and the new function arity;
3. `version` was named among the cells that kill the blanket-classifier mutation — it is an exit-0 SUCCESS report through `output::emit_report`, which this decision does not touch, so it stays green and pins nothing. Verified in passing that `doctor` IS a genuine killer (migrate_doctor.rs:490-513 asserts a structured error on stdout), so only `version` was wrong;
4. the deferral of the new gate script to the implementation commit is CORRECT but was justified by a false rule; the true rule is that a required-STEP ENUMERATION must not list a step absent from the tree, while ordinary prose may name a planned one.

RE-VERIFIED after the hand pass: doc-lint OK (19 docs, 6 classes clean), the five required check scripts green (d43, d44, ub-lp9.25, d46, d47), check-layering green, and the two hand-fixed false strings confirmed gone.

DEFERRED TO THE IMPLEMENTATION COMMIT, inherited by the Implement phase and checkable at the Verify gate: the new gate script scripts/checks/d48-stdout-channel-claims.sh and the prose that names it in ci-cd section 2.1, PROCESS section 3 and the CI workflow — following the verified D47 precedent, where the PRD named the script in the spec commit and the enumeration edits landed with the implementation.

FOUR RESIDUALS NOW NAMED IN THE DECISION ROW RATHER THAN IMPLIED CLOSED: ub-kp7 (the server still dies on a first frame that is neither `initialize` nor `ping`), ub-b1a (the message still embeds an unbounded `Debug` rendering of client bytes), ub-c5o (`output::emit_report` writes to stdout with no notion of a stdout-owning command — latent, since no live path reaches it from `mcp`), and ub-5v5 (no response-size cap, so a large frame may be written truncated — reasoned from source and never reproduced, and stated in that register).

THE REAL ONE, and the orchestrator MEASURED it rather than taking the gate at its word. The self-test that claimed to pin `wait_for` joining its drain threads did not pin it, and said in its own docstring that it "reads the SYNCHRONISATION, not its outcome". It read the length of the handle vector — which `join_drains` empties with `drain(..)` whether or not it joins. Replacing `handle.join()` with `drop(handle)` was applied and the WHOLE unblock-cli crate stayed green at cargo exit 0. That was the SECOND escape of this same pin: the earlier mutation round closed "delete the call" and never covered "gut the body". The repaired cell now uses a grandchild that writes a second AFTER the child exits, so an unjoined drain provably has not read those bytes — an observation the mutation cannot fabricate, unlike a side effect it reproduced exactly. Re-measured after the fix: both mutations turn it red at cargo exit 101, and so does gating the join on a successful exit (the new fixture exits 1, which the old one did not).

THE FIVE PROSE ONES: a claim that one cell was the only in-process guard when three are; stdout purity claimed for "the WHOLE command" and "EVERY path" when `--help` is carved out by decision and a shipped test asserts it; a derived count wrong in both halves; roughly twenty stale file:line anchors in the decision row, one pointing at a different function entirely; and a gate-script row satisfiable by a doc comment rather than by the production line it claimed to pin.

description:
Found 2026-08-05 by the ub-cnv Understand phase and verified directly by the orchestrator. Miguel scoped it OUT of ub-cnv and into its own issue: ub-cnv's fix removes one WAY of reaching this, but the defect itself is about which channel the error is written to, and that is reachable by other routes and touches D40's teardown contract.

REPRODUCED. Start the server and make the very first frame anything that decodes to a notification — for instance a frame carrying an undecodable request id, which is exactly the ub-cnv class. rmcp fails the handshake with "expect initialized request", and the process then writes this to STDOUT:

  {"code":"INTERNAL_ERROR","message":"mcp server error: failed to start the MCP server: expect initialized request, but received: Some(Notification(JsonRpcNotification { ... }))","retryable":false}

and exits 1. A clean non-initialize request in the same position is answered normally and exits 0, so the trigger is the degradation to a notification, not the absence of a handshake.

WHY THIS IS A DEFECT ON ITS OWN. On the MCP stdio transport, stdout is the JSON-RPC framing channel: every byte on it is supposed to be a JSON-RPC frame. This blob is not one. A client reading the stream gets an unparseable line where a frame is expected — the server's own diagnostic corrupts the channel it is diagnosing. The repo's own rule (NFR-14) is structured output to stdout and diagnostics to stderr, but for the mcp subcommand the structured-output channel IS the protocol, which the generic CLI error renderer does not know.

The path is crates/unblock-cli/src/exit.rs:133-141 rendering a StructuredError in the json output format, reached because the mcp server-start error maps to ErrorCode::InternalError, whose exit code is 1 (crates/unblock-error/src/code.rs:315). Adjacent decision: D40 already settled the exit code for EOF-before-handshake; this is the neighbouring question of what the mcp path may write, and where.

INVESTIGATE FIRST. Establish every way the mcp subcommand can write a non-frame byte to stdout, not just this one. The handshake-failure path is the one observed; there may be others (panic paths, early workspace errors, the update path).

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- Every non-frame diagnostic on the mcp path goes to stderr; stdout carries only JSON-RPC frames, for the whole lifetime of the process including startup and teardown failures.
- The exit code for a failed handshake is decided explicitly and reconciled with D40, which already fixed the EOF-before-handshake code — either it rides D40's reasoning or the difference is stated.
- A regression test asserts stdout is frame-only on the failure path, and it fails if the blob returns.
- Whatever ships is reconciled with NFR-14, whose "structured to stdout" wording does not anticipate a subcommand whose stdout is a protocol channel.
title: Bug: `unblock mcp` writes its structured-error blob onto STDOUT — the JSON-RPC framing channel — on every startup failure and on a failed handshake

description:
Observed 2026-08-06 by the ub-cnv (D47) implementer while running the full local gate on branch ubcnv-envelope-id-reject. Reported rather than swept: it is unrelated to that branch, which touches no crate below the MCP layer.

SYMPTOM. `cargo insta test --check --workspace --all-features` exited 1 on the unblock-storage test `libsql::tests::open_in_memory_parallel_first_write_stress`, failing with `BackendOpaque("SQLite failure: bad parameter or other API misuse")` raised around crates/unblock-storage/src/libsql/mod.rs:1081. The same test was then re-run five times in isolation and passed 5/5, and a full re-run of the whole suite was green — so it is intermittent, not a deterministic break.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN A NUISANCE. This is the in-memory parallel first-write stress test, i.e. it exercises exactly the contention path that NFR-3 and the M0 contention lab exist to protect, on a data-integrity tool. An intermittent SQLite API-misuse error on that path is either (a) a genuine race in how the backend opens or serializes the first write against concurrent openers, or (b) a defect in the test's own harness. Which of the two it is has not been established, and the difference is the difference between a test bug and a storage bug.

DO NOT assume it is the test. The comparable case already in the tracker (ub-jyf) IS a generator defect, and the temptation is to file this beside it and move on; the failure mode here is different in kind — a backend error surfacing from the library, not a property-test assertion.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
- The failure is reproduced deliberately (a loop over many runs, ideally under load or with a stress count raised) rather than waited for.
- Established from the libsql API contract which call is being misused and by whom: the production open/write path, or the test harness.
- If it is a production race: fixed at the storage layer, with a contention case added to the Storage contract suite (NFR-16).
- If it is a harness defect: fixed in the test, with the reason recorded so the next reader does not re-suspect the backend.
- The test is deterministic-green across a high repeat count locally.
title: Flaky: libsql open_in_memory_parallel_first_write_stress intermittently fails with SQLite "bad parameter or other API misuse"

description:
Found 2026-08-07 by the ub-gwe Verify gate, by MUTATION. Nothing is broken today; this is a latent defect in a required check's reasoning, and it will bite at a future decision cascade rather than now.

THE RATIONALE, quoted from scripts/checks/d44-create-deps-claims.sh (the comment block just above the live-range knob): "WHY ONE OF THE THREE IS ROW-ANCHORED AND THE OTHER TWO ARE NOT. A file-level token check proves the literal is SOMEWHERE in the file. That is sufficient for CLAUDE.md and xtask/src/doc_lint.rs, which carry exactly one occurrence each (the bump site itself)." The same claim is restated on the row itself, which labels the CLAUDE.md entry as sound at file level "because this file carries exactly ONE occurrence, the bump site itself".

WHAT MUTATION SHOWED. Appending a SECOND occurrence of the live decision-range literal to CLAUDE.md left that script — and all four sibling range scripts — at exit 0. Changing the literal to a STALE range did fire the row check red, as designed. So the check enforces PRESENCE of the live range, and nothing enforces the uniqueness the rationale rests on.

WHY THAT MATTERS, precisely. The rationale is not decoration: it is the argument for why this site is checked at file level instead of being row-anchored. The comment itself records that this exact reasoning already failed once elsewhere — the ci-cd document also described the pin in prose, and reverting the normative statement to the previous range left the file-level check green because the prose satisfied it. That is the same failure mode, and the CLAUDE.md site is protected from it only by the accident that nothing has yet added a second mention. A future decision cascade that adds one — entirely plausibly, since these cascades touch prose sites by design — would leave the file-level check green while the bump site itself went stale.

STATE TODAY, verified: CLAUDE.md carries exactly one occurrence, in the document-map row. The ub-gwe change that surfaced this adds none, and the bullet it rewrites contains no range literal.

RELATED: the sibling finding that no executable check anchors the CLAUDE.md hard rules at all (issue ub-lg7). Both concern the same unprotected file and may share one fix.

### Acceptance Criteria
- The site is either ROW-ANCHORED (so the check binds to the document-map row rather than to the file), or the uniqueness the rationale rests on is itself made executable (the check fails when a second occurrence appears), or the rationale is rewritten to claim only what is enforced. Any of the three is acceptable; leaving a required check justified by an unenforced premise is not.
- Whichever is chosen is proven by mutation, in both directions: adding a second occurrence, and staling the live one, each produce the intended result.
- The same question is answered for the sibling site in xtask/src/doc_lint.rs, which the identical rationale covers with the identical wording — do not fix one and leave its twin.
- The comment block that carries the reasoning is left consistent with the code in the same change, since its whole purpose is to tell the next editor why the shapes differ.
title: Chore: the CLAUDE.md D-range check enforces only PRESENCE while its rationale claims "exactly one occurrence" — a future cascade can defeat it silently

description:
Split out of ub-kp7 (D50) by Miguel's ruling at the Verify gate on 2026-09-14: the harness change rides its own change, not the D50 pull request.

WHAT WAS OBSERVED. The repointed D38 witness, a_no_signal_run_loop_error_exits_1_and_never_hangs in crates/unblock-cli/tests/mcp_lifecycle.rs (it closes its own read end of the child's stdout, sends a pre-handshake ping, and expects rmcp's reply write to fail with a broken pipe into a transport error, exit 1), hung once in twelve runs during the D50 implementation under the heaviest parallel load of that session, failing the twenty-second no-hang deadline in crates/unblock-cli/tests/common/mod.rs with only the workspace-bound line on the child's stderr. It then passed eleven consecutive times, and 46 more times at the Verify gate (30 isolated, 10 under a deliberately loaded machine, 6 whole-file runs of the 21-cell suite, the parallel shape that lost it). One hang in 58 runs, never reproduced on demand, so the root cause is unproven.

THE ONE MECHANISM FOUND, read off the Rust 1.96.0 standard library rather than observed. On macOS the child's stdio pipes are created with pipe() and close-on-exec is set in a second step, so a sibling cell's concurrent spawn in the same test binary can inherit this cell's stdout read end. close_stdout() then does not close the LAST read end, the reply write succeeds, no transport error is raised, stdin is held open by design, and the deadline blows with exactly the recorded stderr. Linux uses the atomic pipe2 and cannot hit it.

REMEDY. Hold a process-wide mutex across the child spawn in McpClient::spawn (crates/unblock-cli/tests/common/mod.rs, the spawn call), which closes the window for every cell in the binary at the cost of serialising spawns only. Verify by running the repointed witness repeatedly inside whole-file runs on macOS, and note that no run can PROVE the mechanism, only fail to reproduce the hang. The named fallback if the cell proves flaky on CI is the unit pin an_unsignalled_run_loop_error_keeps_its_0_8_code in crates/unblock-cli/src/commands/mcp.rs, per D50 clause (11), with Miguel as the decider.
title: Chore (test harness): serialise McpClient child spawns behind a process-wide mutex, the one known mechanism for the repointed D38 witness hanging on macOS

close_reason:

comments.text:
Understand + orientation (2026-09-21), off main at 1ff74f2.

graph: used — with a defect worth naming. The codebase-memory index is at 1ff74f2, the same commit as
current main, so it is not stale. Queries by qualified-name prefix answer correctly. Queries by symbol
name do not: search_graph with name_pattern "LibsqlStorage" returned a method in a different crate
(unblock-model ParsedId::is_child_of), and qualified-name results arrive with the name column carrying
markdown headings instead of the symbol's own name. The qualified_name, file_path and signature fields
look right, so the name column alone appears misaligned. Filed separately; the seam reading in this
spike therefore leans on qualified-name queries plus direct file reads, not on name lookups.

WHAT THIS TASK IS. A research spike that must resolve two axes before v1.3 (shared state) can be
locked, and it doubles as the mandatory fresh maturity check that D41 folded into that lock.

  Axis one, where the primary lives: a libsql server (sqld) the team hosts itself, run in Docker
  locally now and self-deployed later, versus the managed Turso Cloud. Miguel's recorded steer is to
  prefer self-hosting so company data stays self-governed, with Turso Cloud as the fallback.

  Axis two, the sync mechanism: libsql embedded replicas versus the newer Turso Sync. As of 2026-07 the
  repository records embedded replicas as production-supported but vendor-legacy, and Turso Sync as
  vendor-recommended but built on a beta engine with a less mature Rust client.

THE CRUX THE SPIKE MUST SETTLE FIRST. The two axes may be mutually exclusive rather than additive.
Turso Sync sits on the new Turso Database engine, and if its server side exists only inside Turso
Cloud, then self-hosting and the vendor-recommended sync mechanism cannot both be chosen. Nothing in
the repository answers this. The desk research has to establish it before any hands-on work, because it
decides whether the recommendation is a sum of two independent picks or a trade between them.

DECISIONS TAKEN WITH MIGUEL THIS SESSION.

  Where the output lands: the recommendation lands as a comment on this issue plus a run-report under

  becomes its own later cascade, a new decision row in the product requirements document section four

PLAN. Desk research first, as a five-lens workflow: the live state of self-hosted sqld, Turso Sync
maturity and whether it can run self-hosted, Rust client maturity for the libsql crate against the
turso crate, the repository seam and what a backend swap would actually cost us, and an
alternatives-and-exit-ramp lens so the spike does not tunnel into two options that may both be poor. A
coordinator then reconciles them into one recommendation plus a concrete Docker-local experiment with
kill criteria written before it runs. The experiment executes second, against whichever candidates
