OPERATIONAL NOTE. The unblock MCP server timed out on session startup because .mcp.json launches it
through cargo run and the debug binary had to compile first. The binary is now built and matches the
workspace version 1.0.1-rc.3. This comment was written through a line-delimited JSON-RPC stdio harness
against that binary.

comments.author: ramosmig
comments.text:
Desk research outcome (2026-09-21), off main at 1ff74f2. Six lenses across two rounds, plus the
orchestrator's own verification of the three claims the recommendation rests on.

=== THE HEADLINE ===

Self-hosted sqld is out. The mechanism axis then collapsed, but NOT for the reason anyone expected: it
collapsed on the Rust CLIENT, not on the server. Both calls now point the same way, and both should be
proven in Docker before the v1.3 lock, not ratified from this desk research.

  Hosting: the self-hosted tursodb sync server.
  Mechanism: Turso Sync.
  Confidence: medium. Three named things block ratification, listed at the end.

=== AXIS ONE, WHERE THE PRIMARY LIVES ===

Self-hosted sqld is ruled out on dated evidence, not on taste. Turso's founder and chief technology
officer wrote on libsql issue #2254 on 2026-07-12 that the libSQL server is in deep maintenance mode
and that Turso no longer runs it in production, having moved to a proprietary server. The last tagged
release is libsql-server-v0.24.32 from 2025-02-14. Seven commits touched the server directory in
twelve months, four of them functional, the last on 2025-12-19. A corruption-after-power-loss issue
opened 2026-07-09 was independently reproduced on 2026-08-18 and is still open. The client-facing port
has no transport encryption at all, since every encryption flag in the server is for inter-node
traffic only. Authentication silently defaults to off when unconfigured, and the official container
entrypoint passes no authentication arguments. For a data-integrity tool holding company data, that
combination disqualifies it as the shared primary. It survives only as a throwaway local fixture.

Self-hosting itself survives. The tursodb binary takes a --sync-server flag, the vendor documents it,
and the server source is MIT licensed in the repository. The Rust client accepts any http:// address.
That server ships with no authentication and no transport encryption of its own, so adopting it means
unblock documents and supports a reverse proxy that its users run. That is a real cost, stated rather
than hidden.

Turso Cloud was priced for the first time in this round and comes out contractually weak. A
multi-member organisation starts at 29 US dollars a month. The bill is driven by rows read, and rows
touched are counted rather than rows returned, which our dependency-graph walks amplify by design. A
security review demanding audited controls, single sign-on or customer-managed keys forces the 499
dollar tier. Bring-your-own-cloud is enterprise-only and unpriced. A search of the whole documentation
corpus for any availability commitment returns nothing at any tier, and the terms of use are dated
March 2024 with liability capped at the greater of one hundred dollars or twelve months of fees. The
conclusion is that Turso Cloud belongs behind a build feature as a documented option, not as the
default and not as the only shared-primary story.

=== AXIS TWO, THE MECHANISM, AND WHY IT COLLAPSED ===

The first round believed the two axes were coupled through the SERVER, reasoning that embedded
replicas need a server only sqld or Turso Cloud provides. That reasoning is superseded. Embedded
replicas are NOT being wound down on Turso Cloud; that path is documented as fully supported in
production and no end-of-life is published.

The binding constraint is the client. Embedded replicas exist in exactly one Rust client, the libsql
crate behind its replication feature, and that crate cannot pass our own required continuous-integration
jobs.

  VERIFIED BY THE ORCHESTRATOR, not taken from a lens. A scratch crate depending on libsql 0.9.30 with
  default features off and core, replication and tls on produces a lockfile that cargo audit rejects:
  five vulnerabilities and two unmaintained warnings, against an advisory database of 1258 entries on
  2026-09-21. The same procedure against turso 0.8.0-pre.11 with default features off and sync on
  reports zero of each. unblock cannot fix the libsql set, because libsql 0.9.30 pins the older major
  of hyper, hyper-rustls and tonic, so the advisory versions are not reachable by any bump we control.

  The sharp edge: four of the five are in rustls-webpki 0.102.x, which is the exact family that commit
  0e3568a cleared from this repository earlier this month. Adopting embedded replicas would reintroduce
  a class of advisory we just finished removing, and it would do so on BOTH hosting options at once,
  because a self-hosted primary and Turso Cloud need the same frozen client.

So Turso Sync is what survives. Surviving is not the same as being proven fit.

=== WHAT BLOCKS RATIFICATION ===

1. THE CONFLICT MODEL CONTRADICTS A CLAUSE WE ALREADY WROTE. Turso Sync resolves conflicts row-level
   last-push-wins. docs/plans/00-roadmap.md:534 says all writes serialize at the primary, reads scale
   via replicas, and there are no multi-master semantics; :528 forbids queue-and-reconcile in v1.3.
   Last-push-wins is silent multi-master. Two agents editing one issue would lose an edit with no
   error and no hook to intervene. Either the hands-on write-through probe finds a server-authoritative
   write path that preserves the clause, or the 2026-07-07 decision is reopened. That second branch is
   Miguel's call and not the spike's.

2. MULTI-PROCESS ACCESS VERSUS SYNC, UNANSWERED BY ALL SIX LENSES. A Turso database file rejects a
   second opening process by default, and our supported topology is child-per-client. Sync requires
   change-data-capture. The documentation says change-data-capture and multi-version concurrency
   control are mutually exclusive on one connection and says nothing about change-data-capture
   alongside the experimental multi-process write-ahead log. A negative answer kills both calls at
   once, so this is the first thing to test.

3. AN OPEN UPSTREAM BUG THAT HANGS RATHER THAN SLOWS. turso issue #8369 reports the sync engine
   holding a blocking mutex across an await point, parking every worker thread on concurrent connect
   and push. We are async throughout with an in-process semaphore serializing writes, so that shape
   stops the server rather than degrading it.

=== A CLAIM I CHECKED AND AM CORRECTING ===

One lens reported libsql issue #2271 as a live data-loss exposure on the shipped 1.0.0. The issue is
real, open since 2026-08-13 with no maintainer reply, and its version premise holds for us: the
bundled core is SQLite 3.45.1, well before the 3.51.3 write-ahead-log reset fix. The conclusion drawn
from it does not hold.

The race needs a checkpoint running concurrently with another connection's write transaction. Ours
cannot. Session::acquire in crates/unblock-engine/src/session/write.rs:123 takes the in-process permit
and then the cross-process advisory lock, and the returned guard lives to the end of the mutation. The
passive checkpoint fires inside with_immediate_tx at crates/unblock-storage/src/libsql/mod.rs:529,
after the commit and before that guard drops, so it runs while the exclusive lock is held and no other
unblock process can be inside a write transaction. We also set wal_autocheckpoint to zero, so there are
no implicit checkpoints on other connections. The migrate-path TRUNCATE checkpoint runs under the same
lock taken explicitly with a zero timeout.

The residual exposure is real but different and much narrower. Our lock is advisory, so a FOREIGN
process checkpointing our write-ahead log — a replication or backup tool, or someone running the
sqlite3 command-line against the workspace file — reproduces exactly the reported topology and we
cannot stop it. That is a known-limitation and documentation matter, filed separately, not a defect in
our write path.

=== WHAT THE DOCKER EXPERIMENT NOW IS ===

The new evidence shrinks it. Dropped: the sqld authentication probe and the second sqld node, since
sqld is out. Retargeted: the identifier-allocation race now runs two Turso Sync clients each
allocating a child of the same parent and pushing, which turns the abstract last-push-wins clause into
a concrete outcome on our own identifier scheme; the crash-durability probe now targets the sync server
rather than sqld. Run first, because either can close the direction in an afternoon: whether two
processes can open one synced file at all, and whether a write can execute server-side with no
local-write-then-push cycle. Added: reproducing the blocking-mutex bug against our real async shape;
putting the turso crate on a branch and running the repository's actual required jobs rather than a
scratch-crate audit, since the licence allowlist is derived from today's lockfile and a large addition
may turn the dependency-ban job red while the advisory job stays green; and cross-compiling the
cryptography backend across the release triples.

=== WHAT THIS SPIKE DID NOT ESTABLISH ===

Nobody connected to a live Turso Cloud endpoint with real credentials, so embedded-replica support
there is documented and defaulted rather than proven by a connection. Nobody exercised a live
self-hosted sync server, so parity with Cloud on bootstrap, long polling and partial sync is inferred
from a same-protocol claim. Whether the sync wire protocol is versioned across client and server is
unknown, so a newer client meeting an older self-hosted server is an untested outcome. Whether the five
libsql advisories are reachable from the embedded-replica code path is unknown, because the audit is
graph-level; this does not soften the call, since a required job going red is a fact regardless of
reachability.

=== SEPARATELY FILED ===

ub-jv2, the cargo feature we named remote maps to the wrong libsql constructor. Verified directly
against the vendored crate. Not to be closed independently of the v1.3 lock, because the correct
mapping depends on which direction wins.

comments.author: ramosmig
comments.text:
Miguel's reframing (2026-09-22), and the orchestrator's correction that follows from it.

THE CORRECTION. The research framed this as two axes, where the primary lives and which sync mechanism
carries it, and treated the Docker container as a way to de-risk self-hosting as a DEPLOYMENT. Miguel
rejected that framing and the rejection is right. It conflated product modes with implementation
mechanisms.

THE PRODUCT HAS TWO MODES, not three shapes.

  Local mode. The workspace is a SQLite file on one machine. This is unblock today, and the
  multi-process topology matters because several processes share that file.

  Remote mode. The workspace is a database in Turso. Writes go there and every developer connected to
  the same database sees the data. Whether several local processes run is not a question in this mode,
  because they are not sharing a file.

THE DOCKER CONTAINER IS A TEST FIXTURE, not a deployment decision. Its purpose is to exercise remote
mode locally without opening a Turso account yet. It is not a commitment to self-deploy, and the
question of self-hosting in production is deferred rather than answered here.

WHAT THAT SETTLES. The self-hosted sync server shipping without authentication and without transport
encryption stops being a blocker for this spike. It becomes a deployment concern that only returns if
self-hosting in production is ever chosen. The hosting axis as the research posed it therefore
dissolves, and the earlier hosting recommendation should be read as deferred, not as standing.

WHAT IT DOES NOT SETTLE, and why the central finding survives intact. Remote mode still has to be
built, and every route to it runs through the frozen libsql crate. Audited on 2026-09-21 and again on
2026-09-22 by the orchestrator: libsql 0.9.30 with core, replication and tls reports five
vulnerabilities; the same crate with core, remote and tls, which is the pure-remote route with no
replica at all, reports the SAME five. They come from the HTTP and TLS stack the crate pins, so the
remote feature drags them in exactly as the replication feature does, and unblock cannot bump past
them. The turso crate offers no remote route at all: its public surface is batch, connection, params,
transaction and value, plus a sync module behind a feature, so it is a local engine with push and pull
and nothing else. This is not a deployment detail. It decides whether remote mode is buildable as
things stand.

THE LIKELY WAY OUT, to be tested rather than assumed. Speak the HTTP protocol directly with our own
client instead of through the libsql crate. The pipeline endpoint is HTTP with JSON, and the HTTP and
TLS versions already in our lockfile carry no advisories. The first Docker probe therefore becomes the
most valuable one: whether a write sent to the pipeline endpoint executes server-side with no
local-write-then-push cycle.

ONE DECISION LEFT WITH MIGUEL, deliberately not asked yet because the probe may close it. Within remote
mode there are two readings. Either every read goes to the server, so all developers see the same
instant and nothing works offline, or a local copy is kept and synced, which accepts a small lag and
keeps offline reads working. Miguel leans toward the first. docs/plans/00-roadmap.md has the second
written as contract, with reads staying local and offline meaning read-only. If the probe shows the
first is viable, that clause is reopened WITH Miguel rather than quietly amended.

comments.author: ramosmig
comments.text:
Docker probe result + a CORRECTION to this issue's earlier comment (2026-09-22).

=== THE CORRECTION, first, because an earlier comment on this issue is wrong ===

The desk-research comment on this issue stated that every route to remote mode runs through the frozen
libsql crate and therefore inherits five unfixable advisories. That conclusion does not hold. Miguel
pointed at the vendor's own Rust quickstart, which documents a remote-only mode on a FOURTH crate the
research never examined: turso_serverless. The research looked at libsql and turso and generalised from
those two. That generalisation was the error.

turso_serverless 0.1.3, audited by the orchestrator on 2026-09-22 against the current advisory
database: ZERO vulnerabilities and ZERO warnings, across 183 transitive crates. Published by Turso from
the tursodatabase/turso monorepo, MIT licensed, described as a serverless driver speaking SQL over HTTP.

Its surface answers the two things unblock actually needs from a remote backend.

  Interactive transactions that live at the SERVER across multiple HTTP requests, held open by a baton
  per section 4.7 of the published protocol. TransactionBehavior offers Deferred, Immediate, Exclusive
  and Concurrent, so BEGIN IMMEDIATE, the exact behaviour our write path uses today, is available
  unchanged.

  Builder::new_remote accepts http:// and https:// as well as libsql:// and turso://, so it points at
  a local container, and with_auth_token_fn takes an async callback, which fits the rule that a token
  comes from the environment or a keychain and never from a config file.

The maturity caveat stands and is not small. First published 2026-07-26, four releases through 0.1.3
on 2026-09-04, 5777 downloads in total. It is young and barely adopted. The risk is real but it is the
opposite KIND of risk to libsql's: this crate is being actively developed, that one is frozen.

=== THE PROBE ===

Ran against ghcr.io/tursodatabase/libsql-server in Docker on 127.0.0.1:8080, standalone node, no
account and no credentials. The container is a TEST FIXTURE for remote mode, per Miguel's framing, not
a proposal to deploy sqld.

Result, all four:

  1. A write sent by client A executed at the server and was accepted.
  2. An independent client B, built separately, read that row back with no sync call of any kind.
  3. Eight concurrent writers each performed twelve allocations in the real unblock shape, reading the
     high-water mark and inserting high-water plus one inside ONE server-held transaction. Result: 96
     committed, 96 unique, exactly 1 through 96, no duplicate, no gap, zero insert conflicts.
  4. No database file of any kind appeared in the working directory, before or after.

THE CONTROL, because a concurrency test that passes first try deserves suspicion. Re-run with the only
change being Deferred in place of Immediate: 12 committed, 84 insert conflicts. So the writers genuinely
overlapped and the assertion has a real failure mode. The clean Immediate run is serialization at the
server, not absence of contention.

=== WHAT THIS SETTLES ===

The id-allocation race across machines is solved by the server, with no lock of ours. BEGIN IMMEDIATE
holds the write transaction at the server for the span of the read and the insert, which is precisely
what our cross-process advisory lock does on one machine and could never do across machines.

The conflict-model objection DISSOLVES rather than being answered. Last-push-wins was a property of
reconciling two local copies. In remote mode there is no local copy, so it never arises, and
docs/plans/00-roadmap.md:534's clause that writes serialize at the primary with no multi-master
semantics is satisfied by construction rather than contradicted.

The multi-process objection DISSOLVES for the same reason. There is no local file for two processes to
contend over.

=== WHAT REMAINS OPEN ===

Offline. Remote mode has none, not even reads. docs/plans/00-roadmap.md writes offline as read-only
with reads served locally. That clause is now the live question and it is Miguel's, not the spike's.

Which server serves remote mode in production. Deliberately deferred, since the container was a fixture.
The probe does show one useful thing about that choice: turso_serverless spoke successfully to a
libsql-server, which is the older server generation, so the client is not tied to one server lineage.

turso_serverless maturity, restated because it is the load-bearing risk now: version 0.1.3, six weeks
old, tiny adoption. No lens has reviewed its open issues, and nobody has run it against Turso Cloud.

Dependency budget. 183 transitive crates in the probe. It would sit behind a non-default feature, but
cargo-deny's licence allowlist is derived from today's lockfile, so a real branch must run the
repository's own required jobs rather than a scratch-crate audit.

=== ARTIFACTS ===

Probe source and both runs are in the session scratchpad. The container is left running as
ubspike-sqld; stop it with docker rm -f ubspike-sqld.

comments.author: ramosmig
comments.text:
Server comparison + the write-pattern result (2026-09-22). Answers Miguel's question of whether
turso_serverless and the tursodb sync server are the same thing. They are not, and the difference
matters less than it first appeared.

=== THE TWO SERVERS ARE DIFFERENT, AND ONE IS NOT A PRODUCT ===

The protocol turso_serverless speaks is documented in the turso repository as "The SQL over HTTP
Protocol, Version 3", with POST /v3/pipeline and POST /v3/cursor, and POST /v2/pipeline accepted for
older clients. It is the Hrana lineage, which is why the client talked to a libsql-server without
complaint.

Measured on 2026-09-22, both servers running locally:

  libsql-server (sqld), the older generation. Serves /v2/pipeline AND /v3/pipeline, both returning
  200. Issues batons, so streams survive across HTTP requests and interactive transactions work.

  tursodb --sync-server, the newer generation. Serves /v2/pipeline only; /v3/pipeline returns 404.
  Every response carries "baton": null, so there are no streams. It rejects the "close" request type
  with "unknown variant close, expected execute or batch", so its request vocabulary is two entries
  wide.

  turso_serverless hardcodes "/v3/pipeline" at session.rs:240 and "/v3/cursor" at :312, with no
  configuration knob. Pointed at the tursodb sync server it therefore fails immediately with a flat
  404. The two cannot be paired at all.

WHAT THE TURSODB SYNC SERVER ACTUALLY IS. cli/sync_server.mdx shows the implementation is generated
from a prompt by a language model, tagged version 0.0.1, with the instruction "Generate simple
implementation of sync server using tursodatabase", and the vendor's sync specification page is
generated from that same prompt. This is a reference implementation, not a server product. An earlier
lens graded the self-hosted sync path "dev-only" and inferred it; this is the hard evidence for that
grade.

=== THE CAPABILITY GAP DOES NOT BITE US, WHICH IS THE USEFUL PART ===

Losing interactive transactions sounds fatal, because the earlier probe proved parent.N allocation
using BEGIN IMMEDIATE held open across requests. It is not fatal, because unblock's write pattern does
not actually need a session. Two probes, run directly against the protocol over plain HTTP so they
work on any server version:

  IDENTIFIER ALLOCATION AS ONE STATEMENT. INSERT INTO alloc (parent, n) SELECT ?1, COALESCE(MAX(n), 0)
  + 1 FROM alloc WHERE parent = ?1 relies only on per-statement atomicity, so it needs no transaction
  and no baton. Eight concurrent writers, twelve allocations each, against each server:
    sqld on /v3/pipeline      - 96 committed, 96 distinct, exactly 1..96, no gap.
    tursodb on /v2/pipeline   - 96 committed, 96 distinct, exactly 1..96, no gap.

  ROW AND AUDIT EVENT TOGETHER, AS ONE ATOMIC BATCH. The mutation invariant is that the issue row and
  its audit event commit together or not at all. Sent as one batch request whose steps are BEGIN
  IMMEDIATE, the statements each gated on the previous step succeeding, COMMIT gated on the last
  statement, and ROLLBACK gated on COMMIT not having succeeded. That is ONE HTTP request, so no
  session is required. Against each server, both halves:
    happy path  - both rows committed, on both servers.
    failure path - a NOT NULL violation in the event step rolled the issue row back, on both servers.

FALSIFIABILITY, because a concurrency test that passes deserves suspicion. The allocation harness was
shown to detect the race in the earlier probe: the same read-then-insert shape run under BEGIN
DEFERRED produced 12 commits and 84 conflicts. The rollback assertion has an explicit torn-write branch
that did not fire.

=== WHAT THIS MEANS ===

The blocker is the client's hardcoded path, not a protocol capability difference. Both server
generations can serve unblock's writes atomically and can serialize its identifier allocation. What
turso_serverless cannot do is address the tursodb sync server, because it only ever asks for /v3.

Three ways out, none of them tested yet: ask upstream for a configurable endpoint path or a v2
fallback; speak the protocol ourselves over the HTTP client already in our lockfile, which is what
these probes did in about a hundred lines each; or accept that remote mode targets a v3 server, which
today means sqld or Turso Cloud.

That third option is the uncomfortable one and it should be stated plainly. The client with the clean
audit only talks to the server generation that the vendor has put in deep maintenance, or to Turso
Cloud, which nobody in this spike has connected to. The newer self-hostable server is a generated
reference implementation that does not serve the protocol that client speaks.

None of this disturbs Miguel's framing that the container is a test fixture. For exercising remote mode
locally without an account, sqld works today and is proven to work by these runs.

=== ARTIFACTS ===

Probe sources in the session scratchpad: the Rust client probe, the single-statement allocation probe,
and the atomic batch probe. Containers and processes left running are ubspike-sqld on 8080 and a
tursodb sync server on 8081 over /tmp/tursodata/server.db.

comments.author: ramosmig
comments.text:
Turso Cloud measured (2026-09-22). This closes the gap every earlier comment on this issue had to
leave open, that nobody had connected to Turso Cloud. Miguel created a free database and supplied a
read-write token, so the fallback column is now measurement rather than inference.

=== AUTHENTICATION ===

The database URL alone is not enough. Connecting with no token is refused at the query with HTTP 401
and the server's own wording, "unauthorized access attempt on database: empty JWT token". With the
token supplied through the client's with_auth_token, the same call succeeds. So remote mode needs a
URL and a token, and the token is exactly the kind of value the credential rule already covers, since
it must come from the environment or a keychain and never from a config file.

=== THE ENDPOINT ===

Both POST /v2/pipeline and POST /v3/pipeline answer 200. That resolves the one thing that made the
client-server pairing uncertain: turso_serverless hardcodes /v3, and Turso Cloud serves /v3.

=== THE ENGINE UNDER IT IS THE NEW ONE ===

A fresh database created through the Turso console today carries __turso_internal_mvcc_meta in its
schema, so it runs the newer tursodb engine with multi-version concurrency control, not the older
libsql engine. Worth recording because an earlier lens reported that a database created without an
explicit flag would be a libsql one. That reading is now stale for new databases, at least for one
created in eu-west-1 on 2026-09-22.

=== THE THREE PROBES, AGAINST CLOUD ===

All three pass, and they pass identically to the local libsql-server run.

  Remote write and cross-client read. Client A wrote, an independently built client B read the row
  back with no sync call of any kind, and no database file appeared on local disk before or after.

  Identifier allocation under an interactive transaction. Eight concurrent writers, twelve allocations
  each, each doing the real read-the-high-water-mark then insert shape inside one BEGIN IMMEDIATE
  transaction held at the server: 96 committed, 96 distinct, exactly 1 through 96, no duplicate, no
  gap, zero conflicts. So Turso Cloud honours interactive transactions across HTTP requests, which the
  tursodb sync server cannot do.

  Identifier allocation as a single statement, no transaction at all: 96 committed, 96 distinct,
  exactly 1 through 96.

  Row and audit event as one atomic batch in one request: both rows committed on the happy path, and a
  NOT NULL violation in the event step rolled the issue row back rather than leaving a torn write.

=== WHAT THIS SETTLES ===

The earlier answer to "is a private sqld the same as Turso Cloud" was yes for the application code and
unverified for Cloud. It is now measured on both sides. The same client, the same SQL, the same batch
shapes, differing only in the URL and the token. The choice of server is a deployment decision, not an
architecture decision, and it can be deferred without blocking design work.

The operational difference is unchanged and remains the real distinction. A private sqld means running
a server the vendor has placed in deep maintenance, with no transport encryption on its client port
and authentication that fails open when unconfigured, and operating its backups and upgrades. Turso
Cloud carries none of that operational load and carries instead the contractual weakness recorded
earlier, with no published availability commitment at any tier and terms dated March 2024.

=== HYGIENE ===

The probes created and then dropped issues, children, alloc, b_issues and b_events in Miguel's test
database. Only __turso_internal_mvcc_meta and sqlite_sequence remain, and sqlite_sequence is SQLite's
own bookkeeping for the AUTOINCREMENT column the probe used. The token passed through a chat
transcript and should be rotated in the Turso console.

comments.author: ramosmig
comments.text:
Miguel's decision (2026-09-22). This is the spike's product outcome, decided by him, recorded here as
the durable statement.

=== THE PRODUCT HAS TWO MODES AND THE PRODUCT MUST SAY SO ===

LOCAL MODE. One SQLite file, which is what unblock does today. A solo developer stays here, and so
does a team that does not need to share yet. No network, no server, no account.

REMOTE MODE. One shared database with every developer connected to it. Two supported server options
that the application code does not distinguish between, since only the URL and the token differ: a
private sqld the team runs itself, or Turso Cloud.

=== HOW THE TWO SERVERS ARE PRESENTED ===

As peers in usage, with a dated status note on the sqld option. Miguel chose this over presenting them
unqualified and over making Turso Cloud the default path with sqld as an advanced section.

The note must state that the vendor has put the server in deep maintenance and no longer runs it in
production, that the client-facing port carries no transport encryption so a proxy must terminate it,
and that authentication has to be configured explicitly because it fails OPEN when it is not. It
carries its date and its source, so it can be retired if the situation changes rather than hardening
into prose nobody will touch.

=== WHY BOTH CAN BE PEERS IN USAGE ===

Because it was measured on both, not reasoned about. The same client crate ran against a local
libsql-server in Docker and against a real Turso Cloud database, and passed the same three probes on
each: a remote write read back by an independent client with no local file, identifier allocation
serialized correctly under eight concurrent writers, and a row plus its audit event committing together
or rolling back together. The probes differed only in the URL and the token.

=== THE BOUNDARY THAT IS NOT CONFIGURATION ===

Choosing the SERVER is configuration and can be deferred without blocking design. Choosing between
LOCAL and REMOTE is architecture, because the two modes need two different libraries with no overlap.
Local mode uses libsql with its core feature, an embedded engine with no network. Remote mode uses
turso_serverless, an HTTP client with no engine at all: its dependencies are reqwest, serde, tokio,
base64, bytes, futures and thiserror, it carries no SQL engine of any kind, and its only constructor is
new_remote, so it cannot open a local file even in principle.

Inside unblock that boundary is already provided for. The Storage trait is backend-agnostic by design
and remote mode enters as a second implementation behind it, which is the seam the non-default feature
already reserves. ub-jv2 is the defect in that seam, since the feature carries a name that means
something else in libsql.

=== HOW THIS LANDS ===

Miguel chose to land it NOW as its own spec-first cascade rather than waiting for the v1.3 lock, so the
decision does not age inside a comment while the documents say something else. Tracked separately; that
task carries the full scope including the decision-id range bump.

=== STILL OPEN, AND DELIBERATELY NOT DECIDED HERE ===

The offline clause. Remote mode as measured has no offline at all, not even reads, while the roadmap
states that reads stay local and offline means read-only. Miguel has said offline read-only matters and
asked whether a local cache can serve it. Three ways to hold that cache are on the table and none is
chosen. The design question underneath them is whether the cache is the primary read path, fast but
able to lag, or only a fallback for when the network is down, which keeps everyone seeing the same
instant. The cascade will mark the clause pending rather than invent behaviour.

comments.author: ramosmig
comments.text:
Miguel's offline decision (2026-09-22). This SUPERSEDES his own earlier position in this same thread
and is recorded as a supersession rather than as a fresh statement, so the record does not read as
self-contradictory.

WHAT HE SAID EARLIER in this thread: that offline read-only mattered, and he asked whether a local
cache could serve it. Three ways to hold such a cache were put to him.

WHAT HE DECIDED: unblock does NOT support offline. There is local mode or online mode, and nothing
else.

WHAT THAT MEANS CONCRETELY.

  LOCAL MODE needs no offline story. The database is a file on the machine, so the absence of a network
  is not a condition it can be in.

  REMOTE MODE is online. When the network is unavailable the tool does not work, and that includes
  reads. No local cache is kept, no mirror is maintained, and no read falls back to a stale copy.

  NO CACHE IS BUILT. The three options that were on the table are closed: the turso crate's sync used
  pull-only, the libsql embedded replica, and a mirror of our own fed by the append-only events table.
  None will be implemented. The design question underneath them, whether a cache would be the primary
  read path or only a fallback, is moot.

WHAT THIS RESOLVES IN THE DOCUMENTS. The roadmap's shared-state section currently states that reads
stay local and that offline means read-only, with no queue-and-reconcile. That clause belongs to the
embedded-replica design, which this spike ruled out, and it is now superseded outright rather than
left pending. The ub-b07 cascade was written to mark it pending; that instruction is now obsolete and
the cascade should land the clause as decided instead. A comment on ub-b07 says so.

THE HONEST CONSEQUENCE, stated once so it is on the record rather than discovered later. A developer on
a plane, or on a train with no signal, or behind a failed corporate proxy, cannot read their own issue
tracker in remote mode. For an agent-first tool this also means an agent loop stops rather than
degrades. Miguel has weighed that and chosen it, and the simplicity it buys is real: one source of
truth, no reconciliation, no staleness semantics, and no second engine in the binary.

description: BEFORE locking v1.3 (shared state) do a research spike on WHERE the primary lives + the sync mechanism (Miguel, 2026-07-20). HOSTING options: (A) SELF-HOSTED libsql/sqld — the libsql server per https://github.com/tursodatabase/libsql/blob/main/docs/USER_GUIDE.md; run via Docker LOCALLY to experiment NOW, deploy self-hosted later if we go this way (company data stays self-governed, no vendor lock-in). (B) TURSO CLOUD — the managed service, as the fallback if self-hosting isn't viable. Also weigh the SYNC MECHANISM (libsql embedded replicas vs the newer Turso Sync — vendor now recommends Turso Sync, embedded replicas = legacy) and the Rust SDK maturity (libsql crate vs turso crate, from the D41 research). MIGUEL'S STEER: prefer self-hosted (start a docker-local experiment early to de-risk the biggest lift); Turso Cloud only if self-host doesn't pan out. DELIVERABLE: a spike + a recommendation feeding the v1.3 lock (this IS the D41 mandatory maturity-check gate, now with the concrete self-host-vs-cloud axis). Do this FIRST in v1.3.
title: Research FIRST (v1.3 shared-state): self-hosted libsql/sqld (docker-local) vs Turso Cloud

comments.text:
Understand map (2026-08-07, orchestrator, off main at b562570).

graph: used — the codebase-memory index is ready at head_sha b562570, which is the current main tip, so it is not stale. It had nothing to answer here: every question this task asks is a text question (does a token occur in a given shell/markdown file; is a script path referenced anywhere in the repo), which the CLAUDE.md hard rule assigns to grep rather than the graph. The graph indexes Rust symbols; this task touches no Rust.

WIRING, confirmed. scripts/knowledge/tests/landing-verify.sh is referenced by NO workflow and by NO live document. A grep over docs/, .github/, scripts/, .claude/ and CLAUDE.md for its path or for the phrase "landing verification" returns zero hits outside the script itself. The doc-lint job runs the six scripts under scripts/checks/ plus cargo xtask doc-lint, cargo xtask knowledge-lint and the run-report-gate selftest; landing-verify is not among them. Sharper than the issue text: the script's own header claims "spec: ci-cd-and-distribution.md §2.3", and §2.3 does not know it exists — that section enumerates exactly three enforcement layers (knowledge-lint, the run-report-gate job, the PreToolUse hooks) and names neither this script nor a fourth layer. Its only mention anywhere is the descriptive run-report .knowledge/wiki/runs/2026-07-23-knowledge-layer-landing.md.

THE FOUR FAILURES, reproduced on pristine main at b562570, all four diagnosed. The script has four parts; the failures come from two of them.

Token-allowlist part (three of the four failures). It asserts that files mentioning "knowledge-lint", "run-report-gate", "memory-retire" or ".knowledge" are a subset of a hard-coded per-token file list. Three files added by later, entirely legitimate work are absent from those lists: scripts/checks/d44-create-deps-claims.sh mentions knowledge-lint, and .github/workflows/knowledge-gardener-reminder.yml plus scripts/checks/ub-lp9.25-dangling-blocker-claims.sh mention .knowledge. Pure allowlist rot; nothing is wrong in those three files.

Same-commit-window part (the fourth failure). This is the one the acceptance criteria asked to judge on its own merits, and the verdict is that it is NOT a normative gap. The check greps the phrase "same commit" across CLAUDE.md, docs/PROCESS.md, docs/plans/ci-cd-and-distribution.md and docs/plans/STATUS.md and requires the word "run-report" within a two-line window of each hit. It assumes every occurrence of that phrase in those documents is the run-report same-commit rule. That assumption was true at landing and is false today. Every genuine run-report site still carries its clause: CLAUDE.md line 103 and docs/PROCESS.md lines 23, 141, 156 and 201 all pass. The three sentences that trip it are about DIFFERENT same-commit rules — docs/PROCESS.md line 40 and docs/plans/ci-cd-and-distribution.md line 65 state the D-range cascade ("all in the SAME commit"), and ci-cd lines 78 and 82 state the issues.jsonl re-export and the D46 sequencing split. Correct prose, wrong detector: the check cannot distinguish the run-report rule from the other same-commit rules that have legitimately landed since, and no allowlist edit fixes that — the heuristic itself is the defect.

WHAT IS STILL GREEN, and it is not nothing. The other two parts pass today and are not covered by any other machinery. The zero-live-hits part sweeps for retired draft names, the retired PROCESS section-7 title, stale STATUS.md references in the templates, and the square-bracket audit-marker grammar in landed normative docs. The landed-set part asserts that the seven knowledge-layer scripts exist and are executable, that the index files, the lint module, its corpus test and the two templates exist, that both wiki subdirectories exist, and that .claude/settings.json still has a hooks block. knowledge-lint k1 through k6 do NOT overlap any of this: all six scope over .knowledge/** content (index resolution, orphans, frontmatter, enums, slugs, run-report sections), so nothing else in CI checks a file mode, the settings.json hooks block, or an audit marker leaking into a normative doc.

So the fork is live and goes to Miguel, and it is a three-way rather than the two-way the issue framed, because the four failures partition cleanly by part: the two rotted parts are landing-era, the two green parts are standing invariants.

comments.author: ramosmig
comments.text:
Decide (2026-08-07). Miguel resolved the fork, and he chose neither of the two the issue framed.

RESOLUTION: split the script. The two landing-era parts are deleted; the two standing parts are kept, the file is renamed to its permanent role, specified in ci-cd-and-distribution.md §2.3 as the layer that section is currently missing, and wired as a step of the required doc-lint job.

What is deleted and why. The token-allowlist part goes because it is not an invariant, it is maintained state: every future file that legitimately mentions .knowledge or knowledge-lint would have to edit it, which is a standing tax paid for a property nothing else asserts is valuable. The same-commit-window part goes because it is unfixable in its own terms, not merely rotted — no allowlist edit teaches a two-line grep window the difference between the run-report same-commit rule and the D-range cascade, the issues.jsonl re-export rule and the D46 sequencing split, all of which legitimately say "same commit" in the same four documents. Its three current false positives are correct prose.

What is kept and why. The zero-live-hits sweep and the landed-set part are green today, are genuine standing invariants rather than one-off landing assertions, and are covered by nothing else in CI: knowledge-lint k1 through k6 all scope over .knowledge/** content, so no other job checks a file mode, the .claude/settings.json hooks block, or the square-bracket audit-marker grammar leaking into a normative document.

Consequences that must land in the same change, stated now so no phase rediscovers them. ci-cd-and-distribution.md §2.3 currently enumerates exactly three enforcement layers in its intro and closes with a named-residuals subsection; adding a fourth layer edits that enumeration, adds the subsection, and updates the §2 job-table row for doc-lint, which today lists that job's knowledge-layer steps by name and would otherwise not name the new one. That document is in the doc-lint corpus, so its own lint sees the edit.

Explicitly NOT triggered: no D-id is minted, so the D-range cascade and its per-script knob rule are untouched, and the new script must NOT acquire a range knob. The precedent is exact — run-report-gate-selftest.sh is already a required doc-lint step carrying no such knob.

Also settled by Miguel's choice, and worth stating because it is the one thing a reviewer might otherwise flag: the 2026-07-23 knowledge-layer-landing run-report names the old filename and is left untouched. It is a descriptive record of a past run and remains accurate about that run; the rename does not make it false.

Next: Spec/Plan then the design Review gate, both adversarial, before any implementation.

comments.author: ramosmig
comments.text:
Design Review gate, round 1: FAIL. Three adversarial lenses (executable correctness, document drift, process and scope) plus a coordinator; eleven must-fixes survived adjudication. The orchestrator independently re-verified the three hardest before accepting the verdict, and all three are real.

The two blockers worth recording permanently, because both would have shipped red.

First, a phrase this repo forbids. The draft spec mandated the wording "mints no decision id" at three landing sites (the new script header, the CI step comment, the new subsection). That exact framing is one of the forbidden-framing families in scripts/checks/ub-lp9.25-dangling-blocker-claims.sh, a step of the required doc-lint job; its regex catches both that spelling and the passive "no D-id is minted", its only escape is a D45 cross-reference that would be false here, and its allowlist is exactly two paths, neither of which is a script or a plan document. Writing the sentence would have turned a required job red on the very commit that wires the new step. Resolution: state the property without the forbidden nouns — the check pins no decision range, therefore carries no D-range knob, with run-report-gate-selftest.sh as the precedent.

Second, a false justification. The draft argued the new layer is needed because nothing in CI notices if a layer script is deleted or loses its executable bit. That is refuted by scripts/knowledge/tests/run-report-gate-selftest.sh, which already tests the executable bit of scripts/knowledge/run-report-gate.sh and is already a doc-lint step. The justification must narrow to the genuine residual: the three hook scripts, memory-retire.sh, the selftest itself, the settings.json hooks block, and the sweeps.

Third, and this is the one that changes the shape of the work. The acceptance criterion demands the failure mode be proven by execution, and two rows cannot be proven that way: the ones asserting the two wiki directories exist. This repo's own PreToolUse bash guard denies any shell command that pairs a mutating verb with the literal .knowledge, so neither the mutation nor its restore can run, and the shapes that would evade it are recorded in ci-cd-and-distribution.md as known bypasses — using one deliberately is not an option.

Miguel resolved that fork: the check gets a SELFTEST SIBLING, following the house pattern this repo already established when it wrote run-report-gate-selftest.sh for exactly the same reason (a gate that cannot be proven by mutating the live tree is proven against fixtures). The selftest builds positive and negative fixture trees rather than deleting anything from the real one, which is guard-compatible by construction rather than by evasion, and it runs in CI, so the proof stays executable instead of decaying into a transcript nobody re-runs. That is the failure mode that produced this issue in the first place.

Two further resolutions taken by the orchestrator and recorded here rather than left to the implementer.

The settings.json hooks assertion is hardened to anchor on the top-level key. The existing row greps for the bare quoted token, which occurs three times in that file, so the natural mutation leaves it passing: the row cannot fail, which makes it vacuous. That is the same class the spec already grew a dedicated non-vacuity row to catch, so fixing it is making the retained row real, not scope creep.

The three presence assertions inside the deleted part are RETAINED rather than dropped. Only the two-line proximity window is broken; the assertions that the same-commit rule still exists at all in PROCESS.md, CLAUDE.md and ci-cd-and-distribution.md are sound standing invariants, and Miguel's split is precisely the principle of keeping what is sound. Dropping them would have been silent lost coverage, which the review lens caught and which is now stated in the record instead.

Round 2 of the gate follows. Under PROCESS.md section 5 this is the last iteration before escalation.

comments.author: ramosmig
comments.text:
Resume (2026-09-07, orchestrator, off main at b562570, one month after the last session).

The round-1 spec draft and six of its eleven must-fixes are LOST: they lived only in the 2026-08-07 session's scratchpad and transcript, both gone. The three comments above are the only durable record. Under PROCESS.md section 5 a failed design Review returns the work to Spec/Plan anyway, so the Spec/Plan is being rebuilt from this record plus the repository (Plan, rust-engineer and project-manager facets consolidated by the coordinator into one implementer-ready spec), and design Review round 2 runs on that rebuilt spec with the same three adversarial lenses as round 1 (executable correctness, document drift, process and scope) plus the coordinator. The five round-1 resolutions the record preserves (the forbidden phrase family; the justification narrowed to the genuine residual; the fixture-based selftest sibling; the settings.json hooks row anchored on the top-level key; the three retained same-commit presence rows) are mandatory inputs to the rebuilt spec; the lost six are to be re-derived independently by round 2.

Lesson recorded for the process: a gate verdict that lists a must-fix count without the must-fixes themselves is not a durable record. From here on every must-fix that survives adjudication is written into the gate comment, not only the count.

comments.author: ramosmig
comments.text:
Spec/Plan rebuilt (2026-09-07). Three facets (landing sites; executable design; process and scope) consolidated by the coordinator into one implementer-ready specification. Shape: scripts/knowledge/tests/landing-verify.sh is moved to scripts/knowledge/knowledge-layer-invariants.sh (0755) with a fixture-proof sibling scripts/knowledge/tests/knowledge-layer-invariants-selftest.sh; both become doc-lint steps appended after the run-report-gate selftest; ci-cd-and-distribution.md gains a subsection 2.3.6 APPENDED after 2.3.5 (never renumbered: the untouchable 2026-07-23 run-report cites section 2.3.5 by number), a count-free layer list in the 2.3 intro, the section 2 doc-lint row naming both scripts, narrowed R-B1/R-B9 residual clauses and a new named residual for the case where both new CI steps are removed together; docs/PROCESS.md section 8 becomes a count-free list naming the check. Two forks went to Miguel and are resolved. (2) Premise correction: the Understand map's claim that nothing else in CI covers the landed-set part is FALSE for exactly four rows: the two index files and the two wiki directories are already asserted by the skeleton guard in xtask/src/knowledge_lint.rs (lines 216-236), and knowledge-lint is a required doc-lint step. It is true for every other row. Miguel keeps the four rows as deliberate redundant coverage, labelled as such in subsection 2.3.6, each with its fixture case.

Design Review round 2 runs on this spec now, with the same three adversarial lenses as round 1 plus the coordinator.

comments.author: ramosmig
comments.text:
Design Review gate, round 2 (2026-09-07): FAIL. Three adversarial lenses (executable correctness, which rebuilt the whole proposed change in a throwaway clone and ran it with mutants; document drift; process and scope) plus a coordinator, all on opus at maximum effort. Ten must-fixes raised, seven survive after merging duplicates and the coordinator re-verifying each against the repository; one lens claim was rejected as wrong (a line-number citation measured on the lens's own edited tree, not on main). The orchestrator spot-checked must-fixes 1, 4 and 5 below against main and all three hold. The architecture of the spec (rename, retained rows, fixture-based selftest, appended subsection 2.3.6, one implementation commit plus a Track commit) is NOT contested by any lens; every surviving must-fix is a predicate or a sentence.

The seven must-fixes, written out so this comment is the record:

1. The retained row that asserts the same-commit rule is still stated in docs/plans/ci-cd-and-distribution.md is a whole-file grep for the phrase "same commit". That file carries the phrase on five lines (65, 76, 78, 82, 95) and only line 95 is the run-report sentence the row's failure message names; the other four are permanent prose about the D-range cascade, the sibling gates' knob sequencing and the tracker re-export. The row can never fail on the deletion it names, and the new subsection the change adds would quote the phrase twice more, keeping the row green by its own documentation. This is the vacuous-row class round 1 already escalated, and the repository fixed the identical defect on the identical file by row-anchoring. Fix: anchor the predicate on a discriminating spelling (the form "same commit/PR" occurs exactly once in ci-cd and once in docs/PROCESS.md), reword the five sites that claim the row pins the intro clause, keep the subsection from quoting the literal the predicate keys on, and give the ci-cd fixture stub the extra non-intro occurrences.

2. The mandated wording calls docs/plans/ci-cd-and-distribution.md an "always-in-context" document. docs/PROCESS.md line 172 defines that set as exactly CLAUDE.md and PROCESS.md; ci-cd is not in it. Fix: drop the qualifier and name the three sites plainly, without a count.

3. Derived counts typed into shipping prose: "three times" / "three-occurrence" for the bare hooks token in .claude/settings.json, "the three hook scripts", "the three same-commit docs", "the two spellings". True today, purely derived, false on the next hook matcher; forbidden by the house rule and by the spec's own wording rule. Fix: use the count-free phrasing the spec already contains.

4. The shipped subsection says the new wiring rows are "two-sided, like every scripts/checks/ sibling". Only four of the six scripts there carry a workflow row and the matching specified-in-ci-cd row (d44, d47, d48, ub-lp9.25); d43 has no landing table and d46 has neither wiring row. Fix: name the four, or ground the rule in ci-cd line 76's own words (a gate cannot ship wired-but-unspecified or specified-but-unwired).

5. Both stated proofs that the layer-count word was removed from docs/PROCESS.md section 8 are vacuous: the word "three" ends line 205 and "layers" begins line 206, so the criterion's regex matches nothing there before or after the edit; PROCESS.md is outside the doc-lint corpus and no row of the new check reads it. An implementer who skips the edit passes both gates. Fix: pair the negative sweep with positive landings (PROCESS.md section 8 names the new script; the ci-cd intro names the fourth layer and the subsection), per ci-cd line 76's own doctrine that a wrapped line is unfindable in principle.

6. Two acceptance probes ("grep -c RANGE_RE on the check equals 0", "no RANGE_RE in the check") read red against a correct implementation, because the sanctioned round-1 sentence ("pins no decision range, so it carries no RANGE_RE knob") contains that literal and is mandated at three landing sites. Fix: anchor both probes on the assignment form, a line beginning RANGE_RE=.

7. The three same-commit fixture documents are specified as one line containing the phrase, while the mandated mutation idiom is grep -v into a new file then mv. On a one-line file grep -v selects nothing and exits non-zero, the mv is skipped, and the case passes where a failure is expected; the executable lens measured exactly two of forty-two cases red for this reason. Fix: give those stubs a second, non-matching line, or drop the conjunction for that mutation.

Advisories worth carrying (non-blocking, full list with evidence in the round-2 report): scripts/checks/d44-create-deps-claims.sh allow-lists only the tracker export, so a wiki run-report about this task sits inside its forbidden-phrase scope and the Track team must be told in section 8; the four wiring rows plus the new named residual widen the enumeration beyond the recorded Decide resolution and are put to Miguel below; the spec's second fork question overstated its premise (more rows than the four skeleton rows have alternative coverage); ci-cd line 360 has a pre-existing drift ("directly after cargo xtask doc-lint", now six steps apart) that the same-session drift policy argues for repairing here.

Under docs/PROCESS.md section 5 this is the second failed iteration of this gate, so it ESCALATES to Miguel rather than looping. Recommendation carried to him: the seven must-fixes are wording and predicate repairs with no architectural dispute, so a single targeted repair of the spec followed by one authorised round 3 is the proportionate path.

comments.author: ramosmig
comments.text:
Escalation resolved by Miguel (2026-09-07). Two rulings.

(1) Path: repair the spec and run a third, authorised round of the design Review gate, rather than advancing to Implement on a failed gate or looping without authority. The repair is a single targeted pass applying the seven round-2 must-fixes and the cheap advisories (including the pre-existing drift at ci-cd-and-distribution.md line 360, under the same-session drift policy), by one implementer on opus at maximum effort; round 3 runs the same three adversarial lenses plus the coordinator and additionally verifies, must-fix by must-fix, that each round-2 item landed.

(2) Scope: the four two-sided wiring rows (the check asserts that ci.yml invokes it and that ci-cd-and-distribution.md specifies it, and the selftest asserts the same for itself) and the new named residual in subsection 2.3.5 for the case where both CI steps are removed together are ADOPTED. Reason: the four sibling gates that carry the pair (d44, d47, d48, ub-lp9.25) establish the precedent, and a check that can ship wired-but-unspecified or specified-but-unwired is exactly the defect this issue exists to close. The Decide resolution is thereby extended, not contradicted.

Standing from the earlier rulings today: the name is knowledge-layer-invariants; the four .knowledge skeleton rows stay as deliberate redundant coverage, and the repair corrects the premise so that subsection 2.3.6 lists every row that has alternative coverage elsewhere, not only those four.

comments.author: ramosmig
comments.text:
Design Review gate, round 3 (2026-09-07, authorised by Miguel): FAIL, four must-fixes. Same three adversarial lenses plus the coordinator, all on opus at maximum effort; all three lenses reported. The executable lens rebuilt the whole change from the repaired spec in an isolated worktree (rename, rewritten check, the selftest with its forty-four cases, both ci.yml steps, all doc edits) and ran the check, the selftest, the four named mutants, the six scripts/checks gates, cargo xtask doc-lint, cargo xtask knowledge-lint, the run-report-gate selftest and the xtask tests: everything green except the acceptance-probe defects below. The orchestrator spot-checked must-fixes 1, 2 and 3 on main and all three hold.

Round-2 ledger, adjudicated: six of seven LANDED (the discriminating same-commit predicates, mutation-proven; the always-in-context label removed; derived counts removed from every shipped sentence; the false sibling generalisation reworded at the sentence named; the RANGE_RE probes anchored on the assignment; the fixture stubs made compatible with the mutation idiom). NOT LANDED: the proof that the layer-count word left docs/PROCESS.md section 8. Its positive half is real and is the strongest addition of the round (two new check rows keyed on durable identifiers: the check goes red until PROCESS.md names it and until the 2.3.6 heading exists, each with a fixture case); its negative half is must-fix 2.

The four must-fixes, written out:

1. Shipped text, one clause. The new subsection 2.3.6 and a row comment inside the check say docs/PROCESS.md is out of the doc-lint corpus "with no sibling gate reading it". False: scripts/checks/d47-envelope-id-claims.sh line 147 and scripts/checks/d48-stdout-channel-claims.sh line 138 each carry a required-landing row over that file, both run in the required doc-lint job, and ci-cd-and-distribution.md says so itself at lines 84 and 86. Same class as round-2 must-fix 4. Fix: narrow to what is true, the sibling gates that read PROCESS.md pin only its section 3 script list, so nothing notices the section 8 layer list going stale.

2. Acceptance-probe table only (never ships). The count-word sweep was widened to a regex that also matches the bare digit at the end of the subsection numbers 2.3.3 and 2.3.4 in their headings, and accepts the singular "Layer". On main it returns three hits, not the one the spec states, and a correct implementation still returns two, so the probe reads red at its own acceptance criterion and invites an out-of-scope edit of two headings. Fix: restore the plural-only, single-space, word-only form.

3. Acceptance-probe table only. The rename zero-live-hits probe omits two exclusions the spec itself mandates: the check's own regex carries the retired literal and the selftest spells it as fixture data (obfuscated test data was rejected as dishonest), and git grep -w matches inside a pipe-delimited pattern. Red against a correct implementation; the tempting repairs undo two recorded resolutions. Fix: give the probe the same four exclusions as the check's retired-name row.

4. Acceptance-probe table only. The always-in-context sweep is the one negative sweep with no positive pair, and its expected output is a judgement ("zero hits in anything this change writes") rather than an output: on main it returns six pre-existing hits in two run-reports and the tracker export. Fix: scope the pathspec so the expectation is a literal zero, and pair it with a positive landing (the 2.3 intro and the subsection name PROCESS.md and CLAUDE.md in the same-commit sentence).

Seventeen advisories, none blocking, recorded in the round-3 report; the ones that matter for Implement: the wiring-section comment text must be given verbatim rather than left for the implementer to invent; two shipped texts contain the literal .knowledge and must land via the editor tools, never via an interpreter heredoc, because of the PreToolUse bash guard; the specification fixture stub must carry the new heading and the check's path on separate lines; probes expecting a zero count from grep -c must state the expected exit, since grep -c exits 1 on zero; git grep's default engine does not honour a word-boundary escape, so no probe or row may be "hardened" with one.

Nothing in the design, the row set, the fixtures, the mutants or the landing plan was refuted in any of the three rounds. Under docs/PROCESS.md section 5 this is the third failed iteration; the next move is Miguel's.

comments.author: ramosmig
comments.text:
Escalation after round 3 resolved by Miguel (2026-09-08). Ruling: the orchestrator applies the four round-3 must-fixes directly (three are edits to the acceptance-probe table that never ships, the fourth is one clause of shipped text), a single confirmation agent on opus at maximum effort verifies that all four landed and rebuilds the change in an isolated worktree to run the whole probe table plus the check, the selftest, the mutants and every CI lint, and on a pass the design Review gate is considered closed and the task proceeds to Implement, with the post-implementation Verify gate (three agents plus coordinator, which re-executes everything) as the remaining net. A full fourth round was declined as diminishing returns: three rounds refuted nothing in the design, the row set, the fixtures, the mutants or the landing plan, and each round's new findings were new instances of the same probe-table classes.

Applied by the orchestrator, each verified against main before editing: (1) the sibling-gate sentence narrowed in the check's row comment and in subsection 2.3.6 to "the sibling gates that read docs/PROCESS.md pin only its section 3 script list", measured at scripts/checks/d47-envelope-id-claims.sh line 147 and d48-stdout-channel-claims.sh line 138; (2) the count-word probe restored to the plural-only, single-separator, word-only form, with bare digits, the optional plural and the word-boundary escape each prohibited in the row, measured on main as matching ci-cd-and-distribution.md line 92 alone; (3) the rename probe given the same four exclusions as the check's retired-name row, measured on main as zero hits; (4) the always-in-context probe scoped to exclude the descriptive archive and the tracker export (a literal zero on main) and paired with a positive probe keyed on the sentences that replaced the label. Also applied on the same rows, from the round-3 advisories: the two grep -c probes state their expected exit, since grep -c exits 1 on a zero count. The spec carries a section 13 ledger recording all of this. The confirmation pass is running.

comments.author: ramosmig
comments.text:
Design Review gate CLOSED (2026-09-08): the confirmation pass Miguel authorised after round 3 returns PASS with no new must-fix. One rust-engineer on opus at maximum effort, in an isolated worktree off main b562570: (a) verified each of the four round-3 must-fixes landed at the sites the spec's section 13 names and that each repaired claim or probe holds against the repository (the two sibling-gate rows over docs/PROCESS.md, at d47-envelope-id-claims.sh line 147 and d48-stdout-channel-claims.sh line 138, anchor only on tokens inside section 3, so the narrowed sentence is true; the restored count-word probe matches ci-cd line 92 alone on main; the rename probe with the check's four exclusions and the scoped always-in-context probe both return nothing on main; the new positive probe has two targets once the intro and the subsection land); (b) swept the repaired sentences with the ub-lp9.25 forbidden families, the count-word patterns and the word-boundary escape: nothing in shipped text; (c) rebuilt the entire change exactly as the spec mandates, machine-compared every shipped text against the spec word for word (identical), and ran everything: the check exits 0 with its OK line and an empty stderr; the selftest exits 0 across all forty-four cases; each of the four mutants is red at exactly its named case and green elsewhere; the six scripts/checks gates, cargo xtask doc-lint (19 docs, 6 classes clean), cargo xtask knowledge-lint (63 pages, 6 checks clean), the run-report-gate selftest and cargo test for xtask are all green; the descriptive archive is untouched; every probe of section 9 matches its expected cell, exit included.

Implement follows, starting from the confirmation rebuild (worktree commit bc5ab04 on top of main), which is already a verbatim, fully green implementation of the spec; the Implement team applies the three notes above, re-runs the full gate list and lands ONE Conventional implementation commit on the task branch. Then the Verify gate.

comments.author: ramosmig
comments.text:
Implement summary (2026-09-08). One rust-engineer on opus at maximum effort, in an isolated worktree, starting from the confirmation rebuild. Result: branch ub-wvh-knowledge-layer-invariants carries exactly ONE implementation commit, 200bbe5, on top of main b562570 (ci(knowledge): wire the knowledge-layer invariants check as doc-lint layer (iv); body names ub-wvh, states that the check pins no decision range and carries no RANGE_RE knob on the same footing as the run-report-gate selftest, and that the run-report and tracker re-export belong to Track). Not pushed, no PR yet. Diff: six files, 741 insertions, 123 deletions: ci.yml gains the two doc-lint steps; docs/PROCESS.md section 8 becomes a count-free layer list naming the check; docs/plans/ci-cd-and-distribution.md gains the count-free 2.3 intro, the section 2 job-table row, the narrowed 2.3.5 residual clauses plus the new residual, the line-360 repair and subsection 2.3.6; scripts/knowledge/knowledge-layer-invariants.sh (140 lines, 0755) replaces scripts/knowledge/tests/landing-verify.sh (107 lines) by rename; scripts/knowledge/tests/knowledge-layer-invariants-selftest.sh (388 lines, 0755) is new.

description:
Found 2026-08-07 by the ub-gwe Verify gate, measured independently by two lenses in separate private checkouts, and scoped OUT of that change: it fails identically on pristine main and with the change applied, so nothing in ub-gwe causes it.

WHAT IT IS. scripts/knowledge/tests/landing-verify.sh was written at the .knowledge layer's landing (the run-report at .knowledge/wiki/runs/2026-07-23-knowledge-layer-landing.md records it as the executable replacement for a set of self-falsifying prose greps, and records it reporting all checks OK at that time). It is an ALLOWLIST-based check: it asserts that certain tokens appear only in the files that are supposed to carry them.

WHAT IT REPORTS TODAY, verbatim, exit non-zero:
  landing-verify: FAIL — token 'knowledge-lint' appears in unexpected file: scripts/checks/d44-create-deps-claims.sh
  landing-verify: FAIL — token '.knowledge' appears in unexpected file: .github/workflows/knowledge-gardener-reminder.yml
  landing-verify: FAIL — token '.knowledge' appears in unexpected file: scripts/checks/ub-lp9.25-dangling-blocker-claims.sh
  landing-verify: FAIL — a live same-commit sentence lacks the run-report clause in its 2-line window

WHY IT WENT RED WITHOUT ANYONE NOTICING. It is wired into NO workflow. The required doc-lint job runs the six scripts under scripts/checks/ plus the doc-lint, the knowledge-lint and the run-report-gate selftest, and never calls this one; a repo-wide search finds it named only in its own file and in that one descriptive run-report. So its allowlist rotted as later, entirely legitimate work added files that mention .knowledge and knowledge-lint — the gardener-reminder workflow and two check scripts — and no job was there to catch the drift at the commit that caused it.

THE DECISION THIS ISSUE EXISTS TO FORCE, because both readings are defensible and leaving it in the tree unread is the only option that is not: either the script has served its purpose (it verified a one-off landing that is now long past) and should be RETIRED, or the property it guards is still worth guarding and it must be wired into the required job — in which case its allowlist becomes maintained state and every future file that legitimately mentions those tokens has to update it. A checker that no job runs is worse than no checker, because its green is never observed and its red is never seen.

### Acceptance Criteria
- The fork is decided and recorded: retire, or wire into the required doc-lint job. Not left as-is.
- If wired: the four failures above are resolved at their root (allowlist updated, or the check re-scoped so legitimately-mentioning files do not trip it), and the script exits 0 on pristine main. A wired check that lands red is not acceptable.
- If wired: its own failure mode is proven by execution — mutating one allowed file to violate the property makes it exit non-zero on exactly that row.
- If retired: the file is deleted and the run-report that names it is left alone (it is a descriptive record of a past run and must not be rewritten), while any live normative sentence that depends on the script existing is reconciled in the same change.
- The fourth failure — a live same-commit sentence lacking the run-report clause in its two-line window — is investigated on its own merits before either path is taken. It may be a genuine drift in an always-in-context doc rather than allowlist rot, and it would be the only one of the four that points at a real normative gap.
title: Chore: scripts/knowledge/tests/landing-verify.sh has been red since it landed and runs in no CI job — retire it or wire it

description:
Found by the ub-b1a Understand phase (2026-09-09) and split out by Miguel's decision at its Decide phase. Same class of bytes (an unbounded Rust Debug rendering of a client frame) on the same stream (stderr), but a DIFFERENT origin from ub-b1a: rmcp's own tracing, not our error type, and only under opt-in verbosity.

WHAT IT IS. rmcp 1.7.0 src/service.rs renders every frame it receives after the handshake through tracing's `?` sigil, i.e. the full Debug of the typed message: `tracing::info!(?notification, "received notification")` at service.rs:985 and `tracing::debug!(%id, ?request, "received request")` at :942 (plus `tracing::trace!(?evt, ..)` at :851 and the initialize peer_info at :761). Our subscriber (crates/unblock-cli/src/logging.rs:39) builds the directive `format!("{level},{RELIABILITY_TARGET}={level}")`, whose bare leading level is a GLOBAL floor, so rmcp's target is enabled at the mapped level: a single `-v` (INFO) already prints every notification's Debug, and `-vv` (DEBUG) every request's, to stderr, with no cap. A `tools/call` carrying a 5 MB argument therefore lands 5 MB on stderr per frame when the operator turns verbosity on, in addition to whatever the quota later rejects in-band.

WHAT IT IS NOT. Not reachable at the default level (WARN) and not on the pre-handshake path (rmcp service/server.rs:126-257 emits no tracing at all), so it is not a route into ub-b1a. Under the D31 child-per-client topology the host captures child stderr, so an operator running with `-v` to debug a client persists these bytes.

DECIDE FIRST. Whether the CLI subscriber should scope the mapped level to our own targets and hold rmcp's target at WARN unless `RUST_LOG` names it explicitly (this changes what `-v` shows for a reason unrelated to any defect), or whether verbosity is by definition opt-in and the behaviour is accepted and documented. Either answer is legitimate; it must be RULED, not left implicit.

NOT IN SCOPE of ub-b1a's decision, which names this issue as a residual.
title: Bug: rmcp Debug-dumps every post-handshake client frame to stderr at a single -v, unbounded

description:
Found 2026-09-21 by the CI run of PR 444 (ub-kp7), whose diff touches no Cargo manifest or lock. The deny job (cargo-deny advisories) and the audit job (cargo-audit) both fail on RUSTSEC-2026-0285, published 2026-09-14. Both are always-on jobs, not required status checks: the repository ruleset requires only run-report-gate, so a red deny or audit does not block the merge button, it just leaves the run red.

THE ADVISORY. rustls accepted TLS 1.3 handshake messages sent at the wrong encryption level when they followed a key-changing message in the same record, for example a plaintext EncryptedExtensions packed into the same record as the ServerHello. RFC 8446 section 5.1 requires terminating such a connection. The handshake transcript stays authenticated, so a network-position attacker cannot alter or complete a handshake; the practical effect is that a peer can send in plaintext handshake messages that should be encrypted. Functionally the same bug as Go's GO-2026-4340 (CVE-2025-61730). CVSS 5.3. Patched from 0.23.45, unaffected below 0.23.13, so the vulnerable range is 0.23.13 up to but excluding 0.23.45.

MEASURED on main at 11ea156. rustls 0.23.40 enters through hyper-rustls, tokio-rustls, rustls-platform-verifier and reqwest, all funnelling through one reqwest node under axoasset under axoupdater under unblock-cli, so the whole path is the self-update leg. Under --no-default-features rustls leaves the graph entirely. Cargo.lock on the ub-kp7 branch is byte-identical to main's, which is how the same two jobs would redden any pull request opened today.

THE FIX. cargo update -p rustls --precise 0.23.45 resolves rustls 0.23.45, rustls-webpki 0.103.15, aws-lc-rs 1.18.1 and aws-lc-sys 0.45.0, and adds pkg-config. It also re-points six cfg(windows) dependency edges from windows-sys 0.52.0 to the already-present 0.60.2, in errno, is-terminal, rustix 1.1.4, rustls-platform-verifier, tempfile and winapi-util, because each declares a wide requirement that cargo re-unifies when it rewrites the lock. Lock only, 21 insertions and 14 deletions. cargo audit exits 0 over 386 crates and cargo deny check reports advisories, bans, licenses and sources ok, which means no banned crate and no wildcard registry requirement; the duplicate-version knob is set to warn, so it certifies nothing either way. The transitive surface grows by one crate, 385 to 386.

THE TRAP. Plain cargo update -p rustls stops at 0.23.43, which is still inside the vulnerable range. The precise flag is required.

RESIDUAL. All six re-pointed edges are cfg(windows) and every pull-request job runs on ubuntu-latest, while x86_64-pc-windows-msvc is a shipped dist target. That half of the diff is first exercised at release time.
